papers.core_contribution: Introduces two evaluation methods (Contrastive Eval and Sort eval) for assessing the interpretability of sparse autoencoder features, and uses them to show that non-vanilla SAE variants generally outperform vanilla SAEs.
papers.conclusion: New SAE variants are better than vanilla SAEs, validating the evaluation methods, and further development of interpretability evaluations is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Eval and Sort eval provide measures of SAE feature interpretability that correlate with evaluation loss.
Non-vanilla SAE variants (TopK, Gated, Tanh, JumpReLU) perform better than vanilla SAEs on interpretability evals.
The self-explaining method via feature injection works well for early layer features but is less effective for complex concepts and larger models.
Interpretability evals can derisk the adoption of new SAE methods by providing quality metrics.
The evaluations are not comprehensive and measure only a single notion of interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The evals are not comprehensive and only measure a single notion of interpretability, which is nebulous.
The evaluations likely do not have the resolution to distinguish small performance differences between SAE variants.
The self-explaining method succeeds less often on larger models and is sensitive to scale.
future_direction: Creating more and better evaluations for sparse autoencoders.
Using self-explaining techniques as complementary tools in interpretability.
papers.abstract: How can we evaluate the interpretability of dictionary learning features, and do new sparse autoencoder (SAE) variants improve interpretability? Introduces two evaluation methods (Contrastive Eval and Sort eval) for assessing the interpretability of sparse autoencoder features, and uses them to show that non-vanilla SAE variants generally outperform vanilla SAEs. New SAE variants are better than vanilla SAEs, validating the evaluation methods, and further development of interpretability evaluations is needed.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Understanding of Identifiable Sparse Autoencoders and Beyond
papers.research_question: Can SAEs recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the polysemantic inputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical framework showing that standard Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) generally fail to fully recover ground-truth monosemantic features unless they are extremely sparse, and proposes a reweighted SAE (WSAE) that improves feature recovery by adaptively weighting dimensions based on their polysemantic level.
papers.conclusion: SAEs have inherent limits and cannot fully disentangle features under realistic sparsity; they should be regarded as an approximation tool. The proposed WSAE enhances feature recovery and interpretability in low-sparsity scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs generally fail to fully recover ground truth monosemantic features due to feature shrinking and feature vanishing.
SAEs can fully recover ground truth features only under the condition of extreme sparsity.
The proposed Weighted Sparse Autoencoder (WSAE) narrows the gap between polysemantic feature reconstruction and ground truth feature reconstruction, leading to better recovery.
Experiments on synthetic data validate the theoretical findings on sparsity and the improvement from reweighting.
Experiments on real language (Pythia, Llama) and vision (ResNet) models show that WSAE enhances feature monosemanticity and interpretability compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation: SAE-based interpretability should be regarded as an approximation tool, not as a faithful feature recovery mechanism, because full disentanglement is mathematically impossible under realistic sparsity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting features learned by large language models (LLMs). It aims to recover complex superposed polysemantic features into interpretable monosemantic ones through feature reconstruction via sparsely activated neural networks. Despite the wide applications of SAEs, it remains unclear under what conditions an SAE can fully recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the superposed polysemantic ones. In this paper, through theoretical analysis, we for the first time propose the necessary and sufficient conditions for identifiable SAEs (SAEs that learn unique and ground truth monosemantic features), including 1) extreme sparsity of the ground truth feature, 2) sparse activation of SAEs, and 3) enough hidden dimensions of SAEs. Moreover, when the identifiable conditions are not fully met, we propose a reweighting strategy to improve the identifiability. Specifically, following the theoretically suggested weight selection principle, we prove that the gap between the loss functions of SAE reconstruction and monosemantic feature reconstruction can be narrowed, so that the reweighted SAEs have better reconstruction of the ground truth monosemantic features than the uniformly weighted ones. In experiments, we validate our theoretical findings and show that our weighted SAE significantly improves feature monosemanticity and interpretability.

papers.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
papers.research_question: How can we address feature blindness in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for domain-specific interpretability without requiring complete retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Boost, a residual learning approach that trains a secondary SAE to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, enabling selective enhancement of interpretability for specialized domains without full retraining.
papers.conclusion: SAE Boost addresses feature blindness in SAEs, enabling selective domain enhancement without modifying the base model, and represents an important step forward in targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Boost significantly improves explained variance and LLM cross-entropy on domain-specific texts compared to a pretrained SAE alone.
The method maintains general domain performance with minimal degradation, confirming it learns complementary features.
SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Sparse Autoencoder and Activation Difference in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve language model steering by selecting the most relevant sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and applying a token-wise decaying steering strategy to avoid degenerate outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method to select the most relevant SAE feature for steering and introduces a token-wise decaying steering strategy, which improves stability and performance in mathematical reasoning and instruction following tasks.
papers.conclusion: Decaying SAE steering is an effective method for controlling language model behavior, providing a more interpretable alternative to mean activation difference, especially in mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE steering with a single relevant feature and decaying strategy outperforms constant steering and mean activation difference in math reasoning.
SAE steering can elicit step-by-step mathematical reasoning without few-shot prompts.
In instruction following, SAE steering matches the performance of mean activation difference.
The proposed feature selection method effectively removes redundant SAE features.
Decaying steering avoids degenerate outputs such as repetitive words.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method struggles with word inclusion tasks, as no single SAE feature reliably encodes lexical constraints.
The explanations from Neuronpedia are not guaranteed to be precise.
future_direction: Finer-grained SAE combinations for language proximity cases.
Multilingual-aware alignment strategies for steering.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for language model steering. Prior work has explored top-k SAE latents for steering, but we observe that many dimensions among the top-k latents capture non-semantic features such as punctuation rather than semantic attributes like instructions. To address this, we propose focusing on a single, most relevant SAE latent (top-1), eliminating redundant features. We further identify a limitation in constant SAE steering, which often produces degenerate outputs such as repetitive single words. To mitigate this, we introduce a token-wise decaying steering strategy, enabling more faithful comparisons with mean activation difference baselines. Empirically, we show that steering an SAE latent associated with reasoning reliably elicits step-by-step mathematical reasoning and enhances inference quality, functionally resembling the effect of appending a guiding token. Our results demonstrate that SAEs outperform mean activation difference methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and match their performance on IF-Eval.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: Measuring Progress in Dictionary Learning for Language Model Interpretability with Board Game Models
papers.research_question: How can we measure progress in interpretable dictionary learning for language models? The paper proposes using board game models with known interpretable features as a testbed to evaluate sparse autoencoder quality.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces board game models as a testbed for evaluating sparse autoencoders, proposes two new metrics (coverage and board reconstruction) for SAE quality, and introduces p-annealing, a training technique that improves SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a more objective paradigm for evaluating SAE quality with coverage and board reconstruction metrics, and shows that p-annealing improves SAE training.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can accurately reconstruct game boards, though they do not match linear probe performance.
Standard SAEs trained with p-annealing perform on par with Gated SAEs on existing metrics and show improvement on the new metrics.
Coverage and board reconstruction metrics reveal differences in SAE quality not captured by unsupervised metrics like L0 and loss recovered.
The metrics are optimal in the elbow region of the Pareto frontier, validating common wisdom about SAE quality.
papers.limitation:
The metrics are confined to chess and Othello domains, raising concerns about generalizability.
The set of board state properties is determined by researchers based on domain knowledge, potentially overlooking essential features.
The evaluation does not directly address how learned features could be used for downstream interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: What latent features are encoded in language model (LM) representations? Recent work on training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle interpretable features in LM representations has shown significant promise. However, evaluating the quality of these SAEs is difficult because we lack a ground-truth collection of interpretable features that we expect good SAEs to recover. We thus propose to measure progress in interpretable dictionary learning by working in the setting of LMs trained on chess and Othello transcripts. These settings carry natural collections of interpretable features -- for example, "there is a knight on F3" -- which we leverage into $\textit{supervised}$ metrics for SAE quality. To guide progress in interpretable dictionary learning, we introduce a new SAE training technique, $\textit{p-annealing}$, which improves performance on prior unsupervised metrics as well as our new metrics.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: A Survey on Sparse Autoencoders: Interpreting the Internal Mechanisms of Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models. It covers technical frameworks, explanation methods, evaluation metrics, and applications.
papers.limitation:
Incomplete Concept Dictionary
Lack Theoretical Foundations
Reconstruction Errors
Computational Burden
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. Recently, mechanistic interpretability has attracted significant attention from the research community as a means to understand the inner workings of LLMs. Among various mechanistic interpretability approaches, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method due to their ability to disentangle the complex, superimposed features within LLMs into more interpretable components. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of SAEs for interpreting and understanding the internal workings of LLMs. Our major contributions include: (1) exploring the technical framework of SAEs, covering basic architecture, design improvements, and effective training strategies; (2) examining different approaches to explaining SAE features, categorized into input-based and output-based explanation methods; (3) discussing evaluation methods for assessing SAE performance, covering both structural and functional metrics; and (4) investigating real-world applications of SAEs in understanding and manipulating LLM behaviors.

papers.title: From Atoms to Trees: Building a Structured Feature Forest with Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to capture the hierarchical structure of features in LLM representations, moving beyond isolated feature extraction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (HSAE), a method that jointly learns sparse autoencoders and parent-child relationships to extract hierarchical feature structures from LLM representations.
papers.conclusion: HSAE is a novel framework that learns conceptual hierarchies from LLM activations, outperforming post-hoc methods and preserving SAE feature quality.
papers.key_findings:
HSAE recovers semantically meaningful hierarchies from LLM activations, as shown by qualitative case studies and quantitative metrics.
HSAE significantly outperforms post-hoc alignment baselines in hierarchical consistency (e.g., lower Hamming distance, higher co-activation probabilities).
HSAE maintains feature quality and reconstruction fidelity comparable to standard SAEs across various dictionary sizes.
The learned hierarchies manifest geometrically: activations triggering sibling features cluster together in the activation space.
Features with multiple children exhibit higher interpretability (AutoInterp scores) than those with a single child.
papers.limitation:
The tree structure is constrained by a fixed number of levels, which may not fully capture varying depths of semantic abstraction.
Some misalignments in parent-child co-activation persist, and it is unclear if they are due to methodological constraints or inherently non-hierarchical activations.
future_direction: Investigate more flexible architectural priors and scaling laws of hierarchical discovery.
Apply hierarchies for multi-scale model steering and safety auditing.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven effective for extracting monosemantic features from large language models (LLMs), yet these features are typically identified in isolation. However, broad evidence suggests that LLMs capture the intrinsic structure of natural language, where the phenomenon of "feature splitting" in particular indicates that such structure is hierarchical. To capture this, we propose the Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (HSAE), which jointly learns a series of SAEs and the parent-child relationships between their features. HSAE strengthens the alignment between parent and child features through two novel mechanisms: a structural constraint loss and a random feature perturbation mechanism. Extensive experiments across various LLMs and layers demonstrate that HSAE consistently recovers semantically meaningful hierarchies, supported by both qualitative case studies and rigorous quantitative metrics. At the same time, HSAE preserves the reconstruction fidelity and interpretability of standard SAEs across different dictionary sizes. Our work provides a powerful, scalable tool for discovering and analyzing the multi-scale conceptual structures embedded in LLM representations.

papers.title: Kronecker Factorization Improves Efficiency and Interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the computational efficiency and interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for language model interpretation? Specifically, can a Kronecker-factorized encoder with a novel activation function reduce costs while maintaining reconstruction quality and yielding more interpretable features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KronSAE, a Kronecker-factorized sparse autoencoder with the mAND activation function, which reduces encoder computational cost and parameters while maintaining reconstruction fidelity and improving feature interpretability by reducing absorption.
papers.conclusion: KronSAE provides an efficient and interpretable alternative to standard sparse autoencoders, especially in resource-constrained settings, by synergizing Kronecker factorization and logical AND-style interactions to improve feature disentanglement.
papers.key_findings:
KronSAE achieves reconstruction quality comparable to baseline SAEs (TopK, Matryoshka, Switch) under iso-FLOPs constraints while using fewer parameters.
The architecture reduces feature absorption and yields more interpretable (monosemantic) latents, as measured by lower absorption scores and higher automated interpretability scores.
The mAND activation function and head-wise Cartesian decomposition are key design choices that enforce compositional structure and AND-like interactions, improving disentanglement.
KronSAE's pre-latents are often polysemantic, while post-latents are more specific, with retrieval mechanisms resembling logical AND operations.
The method introduces a trade-off between interpretability, efficiency, and reconstruction performance, controllable via hyperparameters (m, n, h).
papers.limitation: KronSAE introduces a trade-off between interpretability, efficiency, and reconstruction performance.
future_direction: Further exploration of the trade-offs and applications of KronSAE.
Developing more sophisticated techniques to identify the fine-grained structure of interactions between pre-latents.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have demonstrated significant promise in interpreting the hidden states of language models by decomposing them into interpretable latent directions. However, training and interpreting SAEs at scale remains challenging, especially when large dictionary sizes are used. While decoders can leverage sparse-aware kernels for efficiency, encoders still require computationally intensive linear operations with large output dimensions. To address this, we propose KronSAE, a novel architecture that factorizes the latent representation via Kronecker product decomposition, drastically reducing memory and computational overhead. Furthermore, we introduce mAND, a differentiable activation function approximating the binary AND operation, which improves interpretability and performance in our factorized framework.

papers.title: Does higher interpretability imply better utility? A Pairwise Analysis on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does higher interpretability of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features imply better steering utility for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds only a weak positive association between SAE feature interpretability and steering utility, and introduces a new feature selection criterion (∆Token Confidence) that significantly improves steering performance.
papers.conclusion: There is a significant divergence between SAE interpretability and steering utility, suggesting that prioritizing interpretability does not guarantee improved steering performance.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability shows a relatively weak positive association with steering utility (Kendall's τb ≈ 0.298).
∆Token Confidence effectively selects features with strong steering performance, improving steering score by 52.52% over the previous best method.
After selecting high-utility features with ∆Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes or becomes negative.
future_direction: Developing advanced post-training feature selection protocols or fundamentally new, utility-oriented SAE training paradigms.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to steer large language models (LLMs), based on the assumption that their interpretable features naturally enable effective model behavior steering. Yet, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does higher interpretability indeed imply better steering utility? To answer this question, we train 90 SAEs across three LLMs (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B), spanning five architectures and six sparsity levels, and evaluate their interpretability and steering utility based on SAEBench (arXiv:2501.12345) and AxBench (arXiv:2502.23456) respectively, and perform a rank-agreement analysis via Kendall's rank coefficients (tau b). Our analysis reveals only a relatively weak positive association (tau b approx 0.298), indicating that interpretability is an insufficient proxy for steering performance. We conjecture the interpretability utility gap may stem from the selection of SAE features, as not all of them are equally effective for steering. To further find features that truly steer the behavior of LLMs, we propose a novel selection criterion called Delta Token Confidence, which measures how much amplifying a feature changes the next token distribution. We show that our method improves the steering performance of three LLMs by 52.52 percent compared to the current best output score based criterion (arXiv:2503.34567). Strikingly, after selecting features with high Delta Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes (tau b approx 0), and can even become negative. This further highlights the divergence between interpretability and utility for the most effective steering features.

papers.title: FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features with Sparse Autoencoders without External Dataset Dependencies
papers.research_question: How does training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on out-of-distribution data affect their stability and feature faithfulness, and can training on the model's own synthetic data improve these aspects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FaithfulSAE, a method to train Sparse Autoencoders on the model's own synthetic data, which improves feature stability and reduces fake features compared to training on external datasets.
papers.conclusion: Training SAEs on the model's own synthetic data (FaithfulSAE) improves feature consistency and reduces fake features, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features.
papers.key_findings:
FaithfulSAEs trained on synthetic data show higher stability across seeds compared to SAEs trained on instruction datasets.
FaithfulSAEs achieve lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models compared to web-based dataset trained SAEs.
FaithfulSAEs outperform web-based SAEs in SAE probing tasks, indicating better reconstruction of the model's hidden state.
Shared Feature Ratio is higher when the target model and source model for synthetic data are the same, indicating that SAE training on its own data is more stable.
papers.limitation:
Lack of evaluation on instruction-tuned or reasoning models.
Shared Feature Ratio may not fully reflect the complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces.
Did not assess the interpretability of individual features through case studies.
future_direction: Exploring improved dataset generation and training strategies that could completely outperform Web-based methods.
Evaluating whether Faithful SAEs provide meaningful and interpretable explanations for individual features through detailed case studies.
Investigating the connection between pruning Fake Features and the principle of Minimal Description Length.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising solution for decomposing large language model representations into interpretable features. However, Paulo and Belrose (2025) have highlighted instability across different initialization seeds, and Heap et al. (2025) have pointed out that SAEs may not capture model-internal features. These problems likely stem from training SAEs on external datasets - either collected from the Web or generated by another model - which may contain out-of-distribution (OOD) data beyond the model's generalisation capabilities. This can result in hallucinated SAE features, which we term "Fake Features", that misrepresent the model's internal activations. To address these issues, we propose FaithfulSAE, a method that trains SAEs on the model's own synthetic dataset. Using FaithfulSAEs, we demonstrate that training SAEs on less-OOD instruction datasets results in SAEs being more stable across seeds. Notably, FaithfulSAEs outperform SAEs trained on web-based datasets in the SAE probing task and exhibit a lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models. Overall, our approach eliminates the dependency on external datasets, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features while highlighting the often neglected importance of SAE training datasets.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Beyond Activation Patterns: A Weight-Based Out-of-Context Explanation of Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we interpret Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features from a weight-based, out-of-context perspective to understand their computational roles, beyond activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a weight-based, out-of-context interpretation framework for SAE features that reveals their computational roles in output prediction and attention mechanisms, complementing activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Weight-based, out-of-context analysis provides the missing half of SAE feature interpretability, revealing computational roles and depth-dependent functional specialization that activation patterns alone cannot capture.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 1/4 of SAE features directly predict output tokens when analyzed through their decoder-unembedding interactions.
Semantic features exhibit a U-shaped distribution across depth in Gemma models (high in early and late layers) and a monotonic distribution in Llama models, revealing architectural differences in functional specialization.
Features actively participate in attention mechanisms, with pre- and post-softmax analysis showing depth-dependent structure and distinct profiles for semantic vs. non-semantic populations.
Weight-based analysis uncovers that early-layer features in Llama specialize for input token recognition (encoder-embedding alignment) while late-layer features specialize for output prediction (decoder-unembedding alignment).
The out-of-context framework provides a complementary, causal perspective on feature function that activation-based methods miss.
papers.limitation:
The out-of-context framework is strict and simulates attention competition across the entire SAE dictionary, which may not reflect the contextual sparsity of actual forward passes and could underestimate feature importance.
The analysis focuses on intra-layer attention (features in layer L interacting with QK circuits in layer L+1) and may miss features specialized for longer-range, inter-layer interactions.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for decomposing language model representations into interpretable features. Current interpretation methods infer feature semantics from activation patterns, but overlook that features are trained to reconstruct activations that serve computational roles in the forward pass. We introduce a novel weight-based interpretation framework that measures functional effects through direct weight interactions, requiring no activation data. Through three experiments on Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 models, we demonstrate that (1) 1/4 of features directly predict output tokens, (2) features actively participate in attention mechanisms with depth-dependent structure, and (3) semantic and non-semantic feature populations exhibit distinct distribution profiles in attention circuits. Our analysis provides the missing out-of-context half of SAE feature interpretability.

papers.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the extent of feature space universality across large language models? Specifically, whether SAE feature spaces are similar under rotation-invariant transformations.
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that SAE feature spaces are similar across different LLMs, supporting the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which enables the transfer of interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that feature spaces are universal across LLMs, providing evidence for the Analogous Feature Universality hypothesis, which can facilitate the transfer of interpretability techniques like steering vectors.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of LLMs show the highest similarity in SAE feature spaces, while layer 0 has low similarity.
Semantically meaningful subspaces, such as those for emotions or time, exhibit notable similarity across models.
The similarity is statistically significant as measured by SVCCA and RSA, with p-values below 0.05 for most layer pairs.
The approach works across various model pairs, including Pythia, Gemma, and Llama models.
Filtering non-concept features and many-to-1 mappings improves similarity scores.
papers.abstract: The Universality Hypothesis in large language models (LLMs) claims that different models converge towards similar concept representations in their latent spaces. Providing evidence for this hypothesis would enable researchers to exploit universal properties, facilitating the generalization of mechanistic interpretability techniques across models. Previous works studied if LLMs learned the same features, which are internal representations that activate on specific concepts. Since comparing features across LLMs is challenging due to polysemanticity, in which LLM neurons often correspond to multiple unrelated features rather than to distinct concepts, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been employed to disentangle LLM neurons into SAE features corresponding to distinct concepts. In this paper, we introduce a new variation of the universality hypothesis called Analogous Feature Universality: we hypothesize that even if SAEs across different models learn different feature representations, the spaces spanned by SAE features are similar, such that one SAE space is similar to another SAE space under rotation-invariant transformations. Evidence for this hypothesis would imply that interpretability techniques related to latent spaces, such as steering vectors, may be transferred across models via certain transformations. To investigate this hypothesis, we first pair SAE features across different models via activation correlation, and then measure spatial relation similarities between paired features via representational similarity measures, which transform spaces into representations that reveal hidden relational similarities. Our experiments demonstrate high similarities for SAE feature spaces across various LLMs, providing evidence for feature space universality.

papers.title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scalably train Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on large language models, and how do these SAEs perform in terms of sparsity-fidelity trade-off, interpretability, and generalization to longer contexts and fine-tuned models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Llama Scope, a suite of 256 Sparse Autoencoders trained on every layer and sublayer of Llama-3.1-8B-Base, along with modifications to Top-K SAEs and a scalable training infrastructure, providing a resource for mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Llama Scope provides a comprehensive set of SAEs that advance the Pareto frontier of sparsity and reconstruction fidelity, and the SAEs generalize effectively to out-of-distribution settings, facilitating future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs outperform vanilla SAEs in sparsity-fidelity trade-off.
Wider SAEs (with more features) achieve better reconstruction quality at the same sparsity level.
SAEs trained on base models generalize well to longer contexts and instruction-finetuned models.
Feature geometry analysis confirms that feature splitting enables the discovery of new features.
The firing frequency distribution of SAE features is consistent with expected sparsity constraints.
papers.limitation:
The monosemanticity evaluation focuses on top activations and may not capture behavior on low-activating samples.
The online activation generation method can lead to redundant computation when training multiple SAEs on the same position.
future_direction: Exploring SAE-based circuit analysis and fine-grained causal analysis.
Conducting automated prompt-based evaluations across a wide range of tasks.
Fine-tuning SAEs for long-context data.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful unsupervised method for extracting sparse representations from language models, yet scalable training remains a significant challenge. We introduce a suite of 256 SAEs, trained on each layer and sublayer of the Llama-3.1-8B-Base model, with 32K and 128K features. Modifications to a state-of-the-art SAE variant, Top-K SAEs, are evaluated across multiple dimensions. In particular, we assess the generalizability of SAEs trained on base models to longer contexts and fine-tuned models. Additionally, we analyze the geometry of learned SAE latents, confirming that \emph{feature splitting} enables the discovery of new features. The Llama Scope SAE checkpoints are publicly available at~\url{https://huggingface.co/fnlp/Llama-Scope}, alongside our scalable training, interpretation, and visualization tools at \url{https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Language-Model-SAEs}. These contributions aim to advance the open-source Sparse Autoencoder ecosystem and support mechanistic interpretability research by reducing the need for redundant SAE training.

papers.title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
papers.research_question: Is the use of nonnegative activations truly essential for the success of SAEs, or does it constrain their ability to capture richer representations? Can SAEs be improved by allowing negative activations, enabling the discovery of bidirectional concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AbsTopK SAE, a sparse autoencoder variant that removes the non-negativity constraint, enabling single latent features to encode bidirectional semantic concepts and improving reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Removing the non-negativity constraint in SAEs via the AbsTopK operator allows single features to capture bipolar semantics and yields reconstructions of superior compactness and fidelity, pioneering a shift towards bipolar sparse representations.
papers.key_findings:
AbsTopK SAE enables single latent features to encode opposing concepts by leveraging both positive and negative activations.
AbsTopK outperforms TopK and JumpReLU SAEs in reconstruction fidelity and interpretability across multiple models and tasks.
AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the supervised Difference-in-Mean method on some steering tasks.
The non-negativity constraint in existing SAEs fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness.
AbsTopK achieves a better balance between safety alignment (HarmBench) and general capability preservation (MMLU) compared to conventional SAE steering.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-step variants, yielding multi-layer encoders that produce more accurate sparse codes.
Investigating JumpReLU variants that apply a threshold on both positive and negative activations.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as powerful techniques for interpretability of large language models (LLMs), aiming to decompose hidden states into meaningful semantic features. While several SAE variants have been proposed, there remains no principled framework to derive SAEs from the original dictionary learning formulation. In this work, we introduce such a framework by unrolling the proximal gradient method for sparse coding. We show that a single-step update naturally recovers common SAE variants, including ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. Through this lens, we reveal a fundamental limitation of existing SAEs: their sparsity-inducing regularizers enforce non-negativity, preventing a single feature from representing bidirectional concepts (e.g., male vs. female). This structural constraint fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness. To address this issue, we propose AbsTopK SAE, a new variant derived from the $\ell_0$ sparsity constraint that applies hard thresholding over the largest-magnitude activations. By preserving both positive and negative activations, AbsTopK uncovers richer, bidirectional conceptual representations. Comprehensive experiments across four LLMs and seven probing and steering tasks show that AbsTopK improves reconstruction fidelity, enhances interpretability, and enables single features to encode contrasting concepts. Remarkably, AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the Difference-in-Mean method, a supervised approach that requires labeled data for each concept and has been shown in prior work to outperform SAEs.

papers.title: AdaptiveK Sparse Autoencoders: Dynamic Sparsity Allocation for Interpretable LLM Representations
papers.research_question: How can we define semantic simplicity or complexity within LLM representation spaces, and how can this be used to dynamically adjust sparsity in sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaptiveK SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on input complexity, improving reconstruction and interpretability without extensive hyperparameter tuning.
papers.conclusion: AdaptiveK SAE provides an efficient and effective method for interpretable feature extraction in LLMs by dynamically allocating sparsity based on input complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Text complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, as demonstrated by linear probes.
Adaptive sparsity allocation based on complexity improves reconstruction quality and interpretability metrics across multiple model scales.
AdaptiveK SAE outperforms fixed-sparsity baselines on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
papers.limitation: Due to cost constraints, the study used a smaller training dataset (250,000 contexts) compared to the 500,000,000 tokens used in SAEBench.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a central challenge for interpretability research. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising solution by decomposing activations into interpretable features, but existing approaches rely on fixed sparsity constraints that fail to account for input complexity. We propose AdaptiveK SAE (Adaptive Top K Sparse Autoencoders), a novel framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on the semantic complexity of each input. Leveraging linear probes, we demonstrate that context complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, and we use this signal to guide feature allocation during training. Experiments across ten language models (from 70M to 14B parameters) demonstrate that this complexity-driven adaptation significantly outperforms fixed-sparsity approaches on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, cosine similarity and interpretability metrics while eliminating the computational burden of extensive hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can we identify functionally important features in neural networks? The paper investigates whether standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) learn features that are functionally important for network performance and proposes a new training method to ensure the features are functionally important.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces end-to-end sparse dictionary learning, a method for training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that ensures the learned features are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted.
papers.conclusion: End-to-end sparse dictionary learning offers a Pareto improvement over standard SAEs, requiring fewer features to explain network performance without sacrificing interpretability, bringing us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately.
papers.key_findings:
For the same level of performance explained, end-to-end SAEs require activating more than twice as few features per datapoint compared to standard SAEs.
End-to-end SAEs require fewer total features over the dataset to explain the same amount of network performance.
End-to-end SAEs with downstream reconstruction loss (SAEe2e+ds) achieve similar performance to SAEe2e while having activations that follow more similar pathways through the network compared to the original model.
The improved efficiency of end-to-end SAEs does not come at the cost of interpretability, as measured by automated interpretability scores and qualitative analysis.
End-to-end SAEs have more orthogonal features and are less prone to feature splitting compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation:
End-to-end SAEs take 2-3.5 times longer to train than standard SAEs.
There is a risk that SAEe2e may take different computational pathways through the network, though this is addressed by SAEe2e+ds.
The automated interpretability score is an imperfect metric of interpretability.
future_direction: Using training tweaks such as a sparsity schedule to allow for higher learning rates.
Using locally trained SAEs as initializations to reduce training time.
Training multiple SAEs at different layers concurrently to reduce training time.
papers.abstract: Identifying the features learned by neural networks is a core challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse, overcomplete dictionary that reconstructs a network's internal activations, have been used to identify these features. However, SAEs may learn more about the structure of the datatset than the computational structure of the network. There is therefore only indirect reason to believe that the directions found in these dictionaries are functionally important to the network. We propose end-to-end (e2e) sparse dictionary learning, a method for training SAEs that ensures the features learned are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted. Compared to standard SAEs, e2e SAEs offer a Pareto improvement: They explain more network performance, require fewer total features, and require fewer simultaneously active features per datapoint, all with no cost to interpretability. We explore geometric and qualitative differences between e2e SAE features and standard SAE features. E2e dictionary learning brings us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately. We release our library for training e2e SAEs and reproducing our analysis at https://github.com/ApolloResearch/e2e_sae

papers.title: Interpreting Large Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse dictionary learning methods (Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations) be scaled and applied to interpret and control large text-to-image diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: This work successfully scales Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) to a large text-to-image diffusion model (FLUX.1), demonstrating they can decompose residual stream activations into interpretable features and enable targeted steering of image generation.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders and Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations are effective methods for interpreting and steering large text-to-image diffusion models, with SAE features being particularly suitable for manipulating concrete semantic concepts in generated images.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and outperform MLP neurons on automated interpretability metrics.
ITDA achieves comparable interpretability to SAEs but tends to encode more abstract visual attributes (colors, textures) while SAE features capture more concrete objects.
Steering image generation via SAE feature activation addition is effective but constrained, requiring the initial prompt to be semantically related to the steered feature.
The residual stream activations in FLUX.1 are highly anisotropic, necessitating PCA whitening for effective SAE training to avoid a high proportion of dead features.
ITDA generally achieves superior reconstruction performance compared to SAEs at similar dictionary sizes.
papers.limitation:
Automated interpretability (autointerp) metrics do not distinguish between abstract visual properties and manipulable semantic concepts, a qualitative difference observed between ITDA and SAE features.
Steering with SAE features is constrained and only effective when the initial image prompt is semantically related to the feature being added.
The autointerp pipeline may have biases, such as picking up on simple image characteristics like color rather than the intended semantic feature.
future_direction: Applying SAEs to vision tasks like classification, segmentation, and depth estimation (sparse probing).
Adapting the SAE encoder architecture to incorporate spatial inductive bias (e.g., convolutional layers) for image data.
Improving steering techniques, potentially by making the process more similar to finetuning or otherwise more aware of steering effects.
Investigating shared features between the text and image streams of the multimodal DiT architecture.
Comparing the two FLUX.1 variants (Dev and Schnell) using methods like crosscoders to find corresponding or unique features.
Investigating biases specific to the automated interpretability pipeline.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are a promising new approach for decomposing language model activations for interpretation and control. They have been applied successfully to vision transformer image encoders and to small-scale diffusion models. Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA) is a recently proposed variant of dictionary learning that takes the dictionary to be a set of data points from the activation distribution and reconstructs them with gradient pursuit. We apply Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and ITDA to a large text-to-image diffusion model, Flux 1, and consider the interpretability of embeddings of both by introducing a visual automated interpretation pipeline. We find that SAEs accurately reconstruct residual stream embeddings and beat MLP neurons on interpretability. We are able to use SAE features to steer image generation through activation addition. We find that ITDA has comparable interpretability to SAEs.

papers.title: Empirical Evaluation of Progressive Coding for Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently obtain high-fidelity, interpretable SAEs of different sizes for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces and compares two methods for progressive coding in sparse autoencoders (Matryoshka SAEs and a permutation/pruning method), demonstrating a trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper discusses the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and interpretability in progressive SAE methods, suggesting that Matryoshka SAEs offer better performance while pruned SAEs offer better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary importance in vanilla SAEs follows a power law.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit lower reconstruction loss and higher representational similarity compared to baseline SAEs.
Pruned vanilla SAEs (via permutation) are more interpretable than Matryoshka SAEs.
Both methods allow efficient progressive coding, with Matryoshka SAEs performing better on reconstruction fidelity.
Feature splitting occurs as SAE size increases, affecting performance when using only a subset of features.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively modest-sized SAEs compared to recent work, and methods remain to be validated at larger scales.
Decoder kernel implementation leads to redundant computations in Matryoshka SAEs.
Feature-splitting presents a limitation when distilling large SAEs into smaller ones via permutation, as selecting only the most important split features fails to capture complete functionality.
future_direction: Validating methods at larger scales.
Improving decoder kernel implementation to avoid redundant computations.
Developing methods to recombine or reverse feature-splitting during distillation.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) \citep{bricken2023monosemanticity,gao2024scalingevaluatingsparseautoencoders} rely on dictionary learning to extract interpretable features from neural networks at scale in an unsupervised manner, with applications to representation engineering and information retrieval. SAEs are, however, computationally expensive \citep{lieberum2024gemmascopeopensparse}, especially when multiple SAEs of different sizes are needed. We show that dictionary importance in vanilla SAEs follows a power law. We compare progressive coding based on subset pruning of SAEs -- to jointly training nested SAEs, or so-called {\em Matryoshka} SAEs \citep{bussmann2024learning,nabeshima2024Matryoshka} -- on a language modeling task. We show Matryoshka SAEs exhibit lower reconstruction loss and recaptured language modeling loss, as well as higher representational similarity. Pruned vanilla SAEs are more interpretable, however. We discuss the origins and implications of this trade-off.

papers.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What causes Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to fail in recovering true underlying features when the features form a hierarchy? The paper identifies and studies the phenomenon of feature absorption.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of feature absorption in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), showing it is caused by hierarchical features and the sparsity penalty, and introduces a metric to detect it.
papers.conclusion: Feature absorption poses an obstacle to the practical application of SAEs for interpretability, and fundamental theoretical issues need to be addressed before SAEs can be used robustly at scale.
papers.key_findings:
Feature absorption occurs in SAEs when features form a hierarchy, causing seemingly monosemantic latents to fail to fire where they should.
The phenomenon is caused by the sparsity penalty in SAEs.
The paper proposes a metric to detect feature absorption and validates it on hundreds of LLM SAEs.
Feature absorption is widespread and occurs in every LLM SAE tested.
Varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve the issue.
papers.limitation:
The absorption metric is limited to early layers (before layer 18 in Gemma 2 2B) because attention moves information to later tokens, making causal interventions ineffective at later layers.
The absorption metric is likely an underestimate of true absorption because it only captures cases where a single latent dominates and the main latents are fully turned off.
future_direction: Develop improved metrics for feature absorption that can be applied at all model layers and capture partial absorption.
Address the fundamental theoretical issues causing feature absorption to enable robust use of SAEs for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) aim to decompose the activation space of large language models (LLMs) into human-interpretable latent directions or features. As we increase the number of features in the SAE, hierarchical features tend to split into finer features ("math" may split into "algebra", "geometry", etc.), a phenomenon referred to as feature splitting. However, we show that sparse decomposition and splitting of hierarchical features is not robust. Specifically, we show that seemingly monosemantic features fail to fire where they should, and instead get "absorbed" into their children features. We coin this phenomenon feature absorption, and show that it is caused by optimizing for sparsity in SAEs whenever the underlying features form a hierarchy. We introduce a metric to detect absorption in SAEs, and validate our findings empirically on hundreds of LLM SAEs. Our investigation suggests that varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve this issue. We discuss the implications of feature absorption in SAEs and some potential approaches to solve the fundamental theoretical issues before SAEs can be used for interpreting LLMs robustly and at scale.

papers.title: Beyond Input Activations: Identifying Influential Latents by Gradient Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Do all activated latents in a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) contribute equally to the model's output, and are only latents with high causal influence effective for model steering?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes GradSAE, a method that uses output-side gradient information to identify the most causally influential latents in Sparse Autoencoders, enabling more accurate interpretation and effective steering of LLM behavior.
papers.conclusion: GradSAE effectively identifies influential latents in SAEs and enables more reliable model steering, with results generalizing across different SAEs and layers.
papers.key_findings:
Not all activated SAE latents contribute equally to the model's output; only a subset has high causal influence.
GradSAE more accurately identifies influential latents compared to a baseline that uses only input activations.
Latents selected by GradSAE are more effective for steering the model's output in a local steering task.
The performance gap between masking top and bottom influential latents is consistent across different model layers and SAEs.
Modifying non-influential (BottomK) latents has negligible impact on model output.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on SAEs trained on instruction-tuned LLMs and one fundamental capability (instruction following for question answering). Extending GradSAE to a broader range of scenarios, including pre-trained LLMs, is noted as future work.
future_direction: Extending GradSAE to a broader range of scenarios, including pre-trained LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as powerful tools for interpreting and steering the internal representations of large language models (LLMs). However, conventional approaches to analyzing SAEs typically rely solely on input-side activations, without considering the causal influence between each latent feature and the model's output. This work is built on two key hypotheses: (1) activated latents do not contribute equally to the construction of the model's output, and (2) only latents with high causal influence are effective for model steering. To validate these hypotheses, we propose Gradient Sparse Autoencoder (GradSAE), a simple yet effective method that identifies the most influential latents by incorporating output-side gradient information.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Capture Language-Specific Concepts Across Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: What language-specific features exist in the feed-forward networks of multilingual LLMs, and how can they be identified and analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-LAPE, a method to identify language-specific features in the feed-forward networks of multilingual LLMs, showing these features are interpretable, influence model behavior, and can be used for language identification.
papers.conclusion: SAE-LAPE can identify interpretable, language-specific features in multilingual LLMs that causally influence model behavior and can be applied to tasks like language identification.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific features exist and are interpretable, primarily located in middle to final layers of the model.
Suppressing language-specific features increases perplexity in the corresponding language, while activating them can shift the model's output towards that language.
Language-specific features can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText, while offering more interpretability.
Features show a hierarchical processing of linguistic information, from morphemes in early layers to complex sentence structures and discourse patterns in deeper layers.
Some features capture stylistic patterns (e.g., conversational vs. formal) and language-specific cultural or geopolitical concepts.
papers.limitation: Interpretations of features may be biased toward the top activating examples, which could come from languages other than the primary one the feature is associated with.
papers.abstract: Understanding the multilingual mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) provides insight into how they process different languages, yet this remains challenging. Existing studies often focus on individual neurons, but their polysemantic nature makes it difficult to isolate language-specific units from cross-lingual representations. To address this, we explore sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for their ability to learn monosemantic features that represent concrete and abstract concepts across languages in LLMs. While some of these features are language-independent, the presence of language-specific features remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce SAE-LAPE, a method based on feature activation probability, to identify language-specific features within the feed-forward network. We find that many such features predominantly appear in the middle to final layers of the model and are interpretable. These features influence the model's multilingual performance and language output and can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText along with more interpretability. Our code and complete figures are available at https://github.com/LyzanderAndrylie/language-specific-features

papers.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate dictionary learning (sparse autoencoders) for language model interpretability beyond unsupervised proxy metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAEBench, a comprehensive benchmark with eight metrics to evaluate sparse autoencoders for language model interpretability, and provides an open-source suite of over 200 SAEs for systematic comparison.
papers.conclusion: SAEBench provides a standardized framework for evaluating SAEs, revealing that proxy metrics are insufficient and that different architectures excel at different aspects of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Gains on proxy metrics (sparsity-fidelity) do not reliably translate to better practical performance.
Matryoshka SAEs perform well on feature disentanglement metrics despite underperforming on proxy metrics.
Scaling SAE width has mixed effects: some metrics improve, but feature disentanglement metrics often degrade except for Matryoshka SAEs.
No single sparsity level is optimal for all tasks; moderate sparsity (L0 50-150) offers a reasonable compromise.
ReLU SAEs are outperformed by newer architectures on most metrics.
papers.limitation: The metrics were designed for evaluating SAEs on the same underlying model, not for comparing SAEs across fundamentally different models such as fully trained versus randomly initialized.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular technique for interpreting language model activations, and there is extensive recent work on improving SAE effectiveness. However, most prior work evaluates progress using unsupervised proxy metrics with unclear practical relevance. We introduce SAEBench, a comprehensive evaluation suite that measures SAE performance across eight diverse metrics, spanning interpretability, feature disentanglement and practical applications like unlearning. To enable systematic comparison, we open-source a suite of over 200 SAEs across eight recently proposed SAE architectures and training algorithms. Our evaluation reveals that gains on proxy metrics do not reliably translate to better practical performance. For instance, while Matryoshka SAEs slightly underperform on existing proxy metrics, they substantially outperform other architectures on feature disentanglement metrics; moreover, this advantage grows with SAE scale. By providing a standardized framework for measuring progress in SAE development, SAEBench enables researchers to study scaling trends and make nuanced comparisons between different SAE architectures and training methodologies. Our interactive interface enables researchers to flexibly visualize relationships between metrics across hundreds of open-source SAEs at: www.neuronpedia.org/sae-bench

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Unveiling Latent Knowledge in Chemistry Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do chemistry language models internally represent chemical knowledge, and can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features within these models?
papers.core_contribution: This work presents the first application of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to chemistry language models, revealing that these models encode a rich hierarchy of interpretable chemical features spanning structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and functional concepts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can decompose the latent representations of a chemistry language model into an interpretable feature basis, revealing a rich landscape of chemically meaningful concepts and enabling causal manipulation of molecular structures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features outperform individual neurons in detecting chemical substructures, especially rare ones, indicating a more disentangled representation.
SAE features provide a compact and decorrelated basis for aligning internal representations with external physicochemical descriptors.
Individual SAE features can capture higher-level functional concepts, such as grouping molecules by shared pharmacological activity (e.g., opioid receptor binding).
Feature steering via ablation demonstrates a causal link between specific features and the generation of corresponding chemical substructures or properties.
The SAE decomposition is information-preserving for downstream tasks (e.g., toxicity prediction) while isolating relevant signals into a more compact set of features than the original neuron basis.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of features remains a presently unscaled process.
The analysis is confined to a single model architecture (SMI-TED).
The features discovered are contingent on the training data's chemical space, and their generalisation to out-of-distribution molecules remains an open question.
While features are compared to the raw neuron basis, more robust baselines are needed to fully validate the decomposition's effectiveness.
future_direction: Developing methods for the automated interpretation of chemical features.
Exploring applications in AI safety, such as identifying and ablating features correlated with undesirable properties (e.g., toxicity).
Investigating how features behave across different model architectures and scales, including exploring concepts like feature splitting.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of machine learning, interpretability has remained a persistent challenge, becoming increasingly urgent as generative models support high-stakes applications in drug and material discovery. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) architectures have yielded chemistry language models (CLMs) with impressive capabilities in molecular property prediction and molecular generation. However, how these models internally represent chemical knowledge remains poorly understood. In this work, we extend sparse autoencoder techniques to uncover and examine interpretable features within CLMs. Applying our methodology to the Foundation Models for Materials (FM4M) SMI-TED chemistry foundation model, we extract semantically meaningful latent features and analyse their activation patterns across diverse molecular datasets. Our findings reveal that these models encode a rich landscape of chemical concepts.
