We identify correlations between specific latent features and distinct domains of chemical knowledge, including structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and pharmacological drug classes. Our approach provides a generalisable framework for uncovering latent knowledge in chemistry-focused AI systems. This work has implications for both foundational understanding and practical deployment; with the potential to accelerate computational chemistry research.

papers.title: k-Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How effective is sparsity by itself as a regularizer and nonlinearity in autoencoders for feature learning and classification?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the k-sparse autoencoder, a fast sparse coding method that enforces exact sparsity in hidden units, and shows it achieves better classification results than denoising autoencoders, dropout, and RBMs on MNIST and NORB.
papers.conclusion: The k-sparse autoencoder is a fast and effective sparse coding method that achieves state-of-the-art classification results by enforcing sparsity alone, without other nonlinearities or penalties.
papers.key_findings:
The k-sparse autoencoder achieves better classification performance than denoising autoencoders, dropout autoencoders, and RBMs on MNIST and NORB datasets.
The sparsity level k controls the locality of learned features; higher k yields more local features, lower k yields more global features.
The method is simple to train and fast for encoding, making it suitable for large problem sizes.
k-sparse autoencoders can be used for pre-training shallow and deep discriminative neural networks, achieving results comparable to state-of-the-art.
A scheduling strategy for the sparsity level during training helps avoid dead hidden units and improves training.
papers.limitation: Too low sparsity level (k) can lead to dead hidden units and features that are too global, not factoring the input into parts.
papers.abstract: Recently, it has been observed that when representations are learnt in a way that encourages sparsity, improved performance is obtained on classification tasks. These methods involve combinations of activation functions, sampling steps and different kinds of penalties. To investigate the effectiveness of sparsity by itself, we propose the k-sparse autoencoder, which is an autoencoder with linear activation function, where in hidden layers only the k highest activities are kept. When applied to the MNIST and NORB datasets, we find that this method achieves better classification results than denoising autoencoders, networks trained with dropout, and RBMs. k-sparse autoencoders are simple to train and the encoding stage is very fast, making them well-suited to large problem sizes, where conventional sparse coding algorithms cannot be applied.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Features for Classifications and Transferability
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features be effectively used for interpretable classification in safety-critical tasks, and what is their performance in cross-lingual and cross-modal transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic analysis of SAE features for interpretable classification, showing that binarized SAE features outperform hidden-state and bag-of-words baselines and demonstrate robust cross-lingual and cross-modal transferability.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are effective for interpretable classification and transfer across languages and modalities, establishing new best practices for SAE-based interpretability in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-derived features achieve macro F1 > 0.8, outperforming hidden-state and bag-of-words baselines.
SAE features show cross-model transfer from Gemma 2 2B to 9B-IT models.
SAE features generalize in a zero-shot manner to cross-lingual toxicity detection and visual classification tasks.
Binarization offers an efficient alternative to traditional feature selection while maintaining or improving performance.
Middle-layer SAE features typically yield the highest classification performance.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is limited to Gemma 2 models and a specific set of safety-oriented tasks; robustness under adversarial conditions or domain shifts needs further study.
The semantic alignment of SAE features with human-interpretable concepts remains an open question.
The toxicity or other safety-related open-sourced data used contained offensive language.
future_direction: Investigate robustness under domain shift, including covariate, subpopulation, and temporal shifts.
Expand the task set beyond safety-oriented binary classification to include multilabel and non-safety tasks and additional multilingual benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide potentials for uncovering structured, human-interpretable representations in Large Language Models (LLMs), making them a crucial tool for transparent and controllable AI systems. We systematically analyze SAE for interpretable feature extraction from LLMs in safety-critical classification tasks. Our framework evaluates (1) model-layer selection and scaling properties, (2) SAE architectural configurations, including width and pooling strategies, and (3) the effect of binarizing continuous SAE activations. SAE-derived features achieve macro F1 > 0.8, outperforming hidden-state and BoW baselines while demonstrating cross-model transfer from Gemma 2 2B to 9B-IT models. These features generalize in a zero-shot manner to cross-lingual toxicity detection and visual classification tasks. Our analysis highlights the significant impact of pooling strategies and binarization thresholds, showing that binarization offers an efficient alternative to traditional feature selection while maintaining or improving performance. These findings establish new best practices for SAE-based interpretability and enable scalable, transparent deployment of LLMs in real-world applications. Full repo: https://github.com/shan23chen/MOSAIC.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control large language model behavior in open-ended generation settings by using supervised steering in sparse, interpretable representation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised steering framework (SAE-SSV) that constrains interventions to a sparse, task-relevant latent subspace identified via labeled data and sparse autoencoders, enabling more targeted control and better preservation of generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SAE-SSV enables effective LLM steering by operating in sparse, task-specific subspaces, outperforming existing methods and providing a more targeted and interpretable approach to behavior control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-SSV consistently outperforms baseline steering methods (CAA, RePe, Top PC, ITI) in steering success rate across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity tasks.
A notably small subspace of SAE latent dimensions is sufficient for effective steering, enabling targeted and interpretable interventions.
Steering in the structured SAE subspace preserves or improves generation quality (lexical diversity, entropy) compared to baselines, which often degrade it.
The method generalizes to unseen datasets within the same task domain, capturing both semantic directions and stylistic patterns.
The top SAE features used for steering are interpretable and correspond to semantically meaningful concepts related to the target attribute.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which may not be available for all models or domains.
Only evaluated on LLMs with up to 9B parameters; scaling to larger models is future work.
Evaluation focused on open-ended generation tasks with limited human evaluation; generalizability to more specialized domains remains to be explored.
future_direction: Achieve universal and style-invariant SSVs that generalize across datasets, tasks, and model families by curating diverse training corpora and developing objectives that encourage semantic steering while minimizing stylistic sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, but controlling their behavior reliably remains challenging, especially in open-ended generation settings. This paper introduces a novel supervised steering approach that operates in sparse, interpretable representation spaces. We employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to obtain sparse latent representations that aim to disentangle semantic attributes from model activations. Then we train linear classifiers to identify a small subspace of task-relevant dimensions in latent representations. Finally, we learn supervised steering vectors constrained to this subspace, optimized to align with target behaviors. Experiments across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity steering tasks with multiple LLMs demonstrate that our supervised steering vectors achieve higher success rates with minimal degradation in generation quality compared to existing methods. Further analysis reveals that a notably small subspace is sufficient for effective steering, enabling more targeted and interpretable interventions. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Ineedanamehere/SAE-SSV.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders: From Shallow Design to Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the limitations of shallow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in extracting correlated features due to an implicit quasi-orthogonality assumption, and proposes an iterative SAE based on Matching Pursuit (MP-SAE) to overcome these limitations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, an iterative sparse autoencoder that unrolls Matching Pursuit, which improves expressivity, learns hierarchical features, and overcomes the coherence limitations of shallow SAEs by enabling residual-guided extraction of correlated features.
papers.conclusion: MP-SAE improves expressivity, learns hierarchical features, and overcomes the coherence limitations of shallow SAEs, providing a foundation for building more interpretable sparse autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
MP-SAE is more expressive than shallow SAEs across varying sparsity levels and dictionary sizes.
MP-SAE learns a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine feature structure, with early atoms capturing digit prototypes and later atoms refining pen strokes.
MP-SAE learns a globally coherent dictionary but selects more incoherent subsets of atoms during inference, unlike shallow SAEs where dictionary and selected atom coherence align.
MP-SAE guarantees monotonic improvement in reconstruction as more atoms are selected, a property not shared by other SAEs.
Shallow SAEs (ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK, BatchTopK) exhibit distinct structural biases in their learned dictionaries, such as ReLU learning full-digit atoms and others learning pen-stroke patterns.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently become central tools for interpretability, leveraging dictionary learning principles to extract sparse, interpretable features from neural representations whose underlying structure is typically unknown. This paper evaluates SAEs in a controlled setting using MNIST, which reveals that current shallow architectures implicitly rely on a quasi-orthogonality assumption that limits the ability to extract correlated features. To move beyond this, we compare them with an iterative SAE that unrolls Matching Pursuit (MP-SAE), enabling the residual-guided extraction of correlated features that arise in hierarchical settings such as handwritten digit generation while guaranteeing monotonic improvement of the reconstruction as more atoms are selected.

papers.title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models
papers.research_question: Can dictionary learning extract meaningful high-level concepts from unsupervised vision foundation models trained on scientific data (cell microscopy images) where prior knowledge about concepts is limited?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ICFL, a novel sparse dictionary learning algorithm combined with PCA whitening, to successfully extract biologically meaningful concepts (e.g., cell types, genetic perturbations) from frozen representations of vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning, specifically ICFL with PCA whitening, is a powerful and promising approach for extracting interpretable biological concepts from microscopy foundation models, enabling new directions for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
ICFL combined with PCA whitening extracts sparse features that correlate with biological concepts such as cell types and genetic perturbations.
ICFL reduces the number of 'dead features' compared to TopK SAEs.
Linear probes on reconstructions from ICFL features preserve significant biological information, with accuracies comparable to probes on original representations.
ICFL features achieve selectivity scores comparable to handcrafted CellProfiler features for identifying genetic perturbations.
Token-level heatmaps from feature directions enable interpretation of subtle morphological changes, such as distinguishing perturbed from control-like cells.
future_direction: Assess whether peak selectivity of handcrafted features can be matched using deep learning-based approaches with fewer non-zero elements.
Future research on interpreting and validating concept directions found in large foundation models for microscopy image data.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we train sparse autoencoders to learn hierarchical features and avoid pathologies like feature absorption and splitting when scaling dictionary size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders, a hierarchical variant that trains multiple nested dictionaries simultaneously to learn features at different levels of abstraction, reducing feature absorption and splitting.
papers.conclusion: Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical interpretability tasks, enabling training of arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Matryoshka SAEs significantly reduce feature absorption and splitting compared to standard SAEs.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve more disentangled latent representations and better performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks.
Matryoshka SAEs maintain or improve downstream task performance with increasing dictionary size, unlike standard SAEs which often degrade.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit a small trade-off in reconstruction fidelity but learn more meaningful features that result in comparable downstream model loss.
The hierarchical structure forces early latents to capture general concepts and later latents to specialize, preserving interpretable features at multiple scales.
papers.limitation:
Slightly reduced reconstruction performance compared to standard SAEs.
Increased training time due to multiple nested reconstruction objectives.
Reliance on quantitative metrics that may not fully capture human-relevant interpretability.
future_direction: Investigate the human interpretability of Matryoshka SAE latents.
Explore the applicability of Matryoshka SAEs to practical interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting neural networks by extracting the concepts represented in their activations. However, choosing the size of the SAE dictionary (i.e. number of learned concepts) creates a tension: as dictionary size increases to capture more relevant concepts, sparsity incentivizes features to be split or absorbed into more specific features, leaving high-level features missing or warped. We introduce Matryoshka SAEs, a novel variant that addresses these issues by simultaneously training multiple nested dictionaries of increasing size, forcing the smaller dictionaries to independently reconstruct the inputs without using the larger dictionaries. This organizes features hierarchically - the smaller dictionaries learn general concepts, while the larger dictionaries learn more specific concepts, without incentive to absorb the high-level features. We train Matryoshka SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and TinyStories and find superior performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks, more disentangled concept representations, and reduced feature absorption. While there is a minor tradeoff with reconstruction performance, we believe Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical tasks, as they enable training arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.

papers.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and steerability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by incorporating user-specified concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE), a framework that prunes low-utility SAE neurons and augments the latent space with a concept bottleneck aligned to user-defined concepts, improving interpretability and steerability.
papers.conclusion: CB-SAE unifies sparse autoencoders with concept bottleneck models, enabling robust interpretation and control of vision representations across modalities and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE neurons have low interpretability or steerability, rendering them ineffective for downstream use.
SAEs often fail to represent user-specified concepts, limiting their practical utility.
CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% over SAE baselines across LVLMs and image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) promise a unified approach for mechanistic interpretability, concept discovery, and model steering in LLMs and LVLMs. However, realizing this potential requires that the learned features be both interpretable and steerable. To that end, we introduce two new computationally inexpensive interpretability and steerability metrics and conduct a systematic analysis on LVLMs. Our analysis uncovers two observations; (i) a majority of SAE neurons exhibit either low interpretability or low steerability or both, rendering them ineffective for downstream use; and (ii) due to the unsupervised nature of SAEs, user-desired concepts are often absent in the learned dictionary, thus limiting their practical utility. To address these limitations, we propose Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE) - a novel post-hoc framework that prunes low-utility neurons and augments the latent space with a lightweight concept bottleneck aligned to a user-defined concept set. The resulting CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% across LVLMs and image generation tasks. We will make our code and model weights available.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Group-SAE: Efficient Training of Sparse Autoencoders for Large Language Models via Layer Groups
papers.research_question: How can the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs be reduced while maintaining performance? Specifically, can grouping similar layers and training a single SAE per group achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Group-SAE, a method to reduce the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs by grouping layers with similar residual stream representations and training a single SAE per group, guided by a novel metric called AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance).
papers.conclusion: Group-SAE provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs, achieving significant computational savings without compromising reconstruction quality, downstream task performance, or interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Group-SAE reduces the number of SAEs needed, cutting training costs by up to 50% with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and downstream performance.
The proposed AMAD metric effectively guides the selection of an optimal number of layer groups, balancing efficiency and performance.
Group-SAEs achieve comparable or slightly better interpretability scores (Detection and Fuzzing) than baseline per-layer SAEs.
Features learned by a Group-SAE are most similar to the baseline SAE trained on a layer within its group, and individual features typically peak at a specific layer but spread to adjacent ones.
The method outperforms alternative efficiency baselines like training smaller SAEs on all layers or using evenly spaced groups, especially on downstream performance metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models from the Pythia family trained on the Pile dataset, and the generality to other architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA) or datasets is not evaluated.
The study uses a fixed expansion factor (c=16) and TopK activation function; the impact of these hyperparameter choices is not investigated.
The interpretability evaluation is limited due to the high cost of annotating large numbers of features; a more comprehensive analysis is needed.
future_direction: Further optimizing the number of layer groups and scaling the approach to even larger models.
Evaluating the method on additional datasets and across diverse model architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral).
Conducting a more comprehensive and systematic interpretability analysis.
papers.abstract: Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs) have recently been employed as a promising unsupervised approach for understanding the representations of layers of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, with the growth in model size and complexity, training SAEs is computationally intensive, as typically one SAE is trained for each model layer. To address such limitation, we propose Group-SAE, a novel strategy to train SAEs. Our method considers the similarity of the residual stream representations between contiguous layers to group similar layers and train a single SAE per group. To balance the trade-off between efficiency and performance, we further introduce AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance), an empirical metric that guides the selection of an optimal number of groups based on representational similarity across layers. Experiments on models from the Pythia family show that our approach significantly accelerates training with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and comparable downstream task performance and interpretability over baseline SAEs trained layer by layer. This method provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs.

papers.title: Dense SAE Latents Are Features, Not Bugs
papers.research_question: Are dense latents in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) undesirable training artifacts or do they reflect meaningful model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Dense SAE latents are not training artifacts but reflect meaningful, functional representations in the language model's residual stream, serving roles such as position tracking, context binding, and entropy regulation.
papers.conclusion: Dense SAE latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the dense-latent subspace in the residual stream prevents new dense latents from being learned in retrained SAEs, indicating dense features are intrinsic to the residual space.
Dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream.
A taxonomy of dense latents identifies classes including position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, alphabet (letter-specific output), part-of-speech, and PCA reconstruction.
The function of dense latents shifts across layers: from structural (e.g., position) in early layers, to semantic (e.g., context binding) in middle layers, to output-oriented (e.g., alphabet) in late layers.
Nullspace-aligned dense latents are causally involved in entropy regulation via interaction with RMSNorm scaling.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a few models (Gemma 2 2B, GPT-2, LLaMA 3.2) and SAE architectures (JumpReLU, TopK).
future_direction: Explore the circuits involving dense subspaces, particularly context-binding latents.
Investigate whether dense latents are a general phenomenon across more models and SAE variants.
Challenge the assumption of globally monosemantic directions and further study context-dependent feature binding.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to extract interpretable features from language models by enforcing a sparsity constraint. Ideally, training an SAE would yield latents that are both sparse and semantically meaningful. However, many SAE latents activate frequently (i.e., are \emph{dense}), raising concerns that they may be undesirable artifacts of the training procedure. In this work, we systematically investigate the geometry, function, and origin of dense latents and show that they are not only persistent but often reflect meaningful model representations. We first demonstrate that dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream, and that ablating their subspace suppresses the emergence of new dense features in retrained SAEs -- suggesting that high density features are an intrinsic property of the residual space. We then introduce a taxonomy of dense latents, identifying classes tied to position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, letter-specific output signals, part-of-speech, and principal component reconstruction. Finally, we analyze how these features evolve across layers, revealing a shift from structural features in early layers, to semantic features in mid layers, and finally to output-oriented signals in the last layers of the model. Our findings indicate that dense latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.

papers.title: From Knots to Knobs: Towards Steerable Collaborative Filtering Using Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to collaborative filtering to extract interpretable features from user embeddings and enable steering of recommendations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies sparse autoencoders to collaborative filtering autoencoders to disentangle user embeddings into interpretable features, enabling steering of recommendations by manipulating these features.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a promising tool for interpretability and steering in collaborative filtering, providing a control panel of knobs to adjust recommendations.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can reconstruct CFAE embeddings with minimal degradation in recommendation performance, especially for cosine-based embeddings.
SAE neurons correspond to interpretable concepts, even when trained only on interaction data without metadata.
Steering recommendations by amplifying specific SAE neurons effectively shifts recommendations toward desired concepts.
papers.limitation:
Basic SAE is sensitive to hyperparameter selection and can degrade performance if misconfigured.
Concept-neuron mapping may have limited granularity due to overlapping tags or popularity bias.
future_direction: Explore the applicability of SAEs to other non-autoencoder collaborative filtering architectures.
Investigate the use of SAEs in broader recommendation scenarios.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as pivotal tools for introspection into large language models. SAEs can uncover high-quality, interpretable features at different levels of granularity and enable targeted steering of the generation process by selectively activating specific neurons in their latent activations. Our paper is the first to apply this approach to collaborative filtering, aiming to extract similarly interpretable features from representations learned purely from interaction signals. In particular, we focus on a widely adopted class of collaborative autoencoders (CFAEs) and augment them by inserting an SAE between their encoder and decoder networks. We demonstrate that such representation is largely monosemantic and propose suitable mapping functions between semantic concepts and individual neurons. We also evaluate a simple yet effective method that utilizes this representation to steer the recommendations in a desired direction.

papers.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do various representation-based steering methods compare to prompting and finetuning in terms of concept detection and model steering for language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AXBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating steering and concept detection methods, and finds that prompting outperforms representation-based methods for steering, while difference-in-means and probes are best for detection, with the novel ReFT-r1 method being competitive on both tasks.
papers.conclusion: Representation steering methods largely lag behind prompting and finetuning, but ReFT-r1 shows that steering can be improved with comprehensive benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting is the best method for model steering, outperforming all representation-based methods.
Difference-in-means, linear probes, and ReFT-r1 perform best for concept detection with no significant difference between them.
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are not competitive compared to other methods on both steering and detection.
ReFT-r1, a novel weakly-supervised method, is competitive on both steering and detection tasks while offering interpretability advantages.
The AXBENCH benchmark enables comprehensive evaluation and comparison of steering methods.
papers.limitation: Hyperparameter tuning might underestimate steering performance due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Extend AXBENCH to arbitrary concept descriptions and add new evaluation tasks as better feature-labelling techniques and steering approaches emerge.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

papers.title: Denoising Concept Vectors with Sparse Autoencoders for Improved Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of linear concept vectors for language model steering by denoising hidden representations using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SDCV, a method that uses sparse autoencoders to denoise hidden representations by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples, leading to improved steering success rates.
papers.conclusion: SDCV effectively mitigates noise in concept vectors and enhances steering performance, demonstrating that denoising representations is a promising direction for robust concept steering.
papers.key_findings:
SDCV improves steering success rates by 4-16% across six challenging concepts while maintaining topic relevance.
SDCV-enhanced difference-in-mean generally outperforms SDCV-enhanced linear probing.
The method is effective across different models (Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B).
Optimal values for top-k and scale factor are not linearly related to peak performance, likely due to superposition and SAE training objectives.
Counterfactual experiments show that amplifying non-top-k latents (noise) generally decreases steering success.
papers.limitation:
The approach is confined to model families for which SAEs have already been trained.
SAEs imperfectly disentangle features and struggle to accurately capture feature importance.
Optimal values for steering strength, k, and scale factor must be determined empirically, which is computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: Linear concept vectors effectively steer LLMs, but existing methods suffer from noisy features in diverse datasets that undermine steering robustness. We propose Sparse Autoencoder-Denoised Concept Vectors (SDCV), which selectively keep the most discriminative SAE latents while reconstructing hidden representations. Our key insight is that concept-relevant signals can be explicitly separated from dataset noise by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples. Applied to linear probing and difference-in-mean, SDCV consistently improves steering success rates by 4-16\% across six challenging concepts, while maintaining topic relevance.

papers.title: Efficient Dictionary Learning with Switch Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders efficiently to reduce compute cost while maintaining performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture that uses a mixture-of-experts style routing to reduce compute cost and memory bottlenecks while maintaining reconstruction performance and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Switch SAEs are a promising approach for scaling sparse autoencoders, providing a Pareto improvement in FLOPs vs. MSE without significant reduction in feature interpretability, and may enable large-scale SAE training on GPU clusters.
papers.key_findings:
Switch SAEs achieve better reconstruction than dense TopK SAEs at a fixed compute budget (FLOP-matched).
Switch SAEs require more total features (parameters) to achieve the same reconstruction as dense SAEs when trained to convergence, but this gap narrows for larger SAEs.
In FLOP-matched settings, Switch SAEs Pareto-dominate TopK, Gated, and ReLU SAEs in terms of reconstruction MSE and fraction of loss recovered.
Switch SAEs exhibit feature duplication across experts, which reduces capacity, but this effect diminishes at larger sparsities.
Switch SAE features are as interpretable as TopK SAE features in FLOP-matched settings, and in width-matched settings they have higher true positive rates but lower true negative rates in automated interpretability detection.
papers.limitation:
Switch SAEs have reduced performance at a fixed number of parameters compared to dense SAEs, especially for attention and MLP layers.
Only the simplest mixture-of-experts architecture is investigated, leaving open the question of maximum performance gain from more sophisticated MoE architectures.
No downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs (e.g., feature steering or circuit discovery) are conducted.
future_direction: Investigate feature deduplication techniques, more sophisticated routing architectures, and multiple active experts.
Explore more sophisticated mixture-of-experts architectures like GShard, DeepSeekMoE, and expert choice routing.
Conduct downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs, such as feature steering or circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a recent technique for decomposing neural network activations into human-interpretable features. However, in order for SAEs to identify all features represented in frontier models, it will be necessary to scale them up to very high width, posing a computational challenge. In this work, we introduce Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture aimed at reducing the compute cost of training SAEs. Inspired by sparse mixture of experts models, Switch SAEs route activation vectors between smaller "expert" SAEs, enabling SAEs to efficiently scale to many more features. We present experiments comparing Switch SAEs with other SAE architectures, and find that Switch SAEs deliver a substantial Pareto improvement in the reconstruction vs. sparsity frontier for a given fixed training compute budget. We also study the geometry of features across experts, analyze features duplicated across experts, and verify that Switch SAE features are as interpretable as features found by other SAE architectures.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: Applying sparse autoencoders to unlearn knowledge in language models
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models in an interpretable way.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that individual interpretable SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models, but current SAE quality or intervention techniques result in similar or larger side-effects than fine-tuning based methods like Representation Misdirection for Unlearning (RMU).
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning is possible but currently has limitations; improvements in SAE quality or intervention techniques are needed to make it comparable to fine-tuning based techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models.
Negative scaling of feature activations is necessary for unlearning; zero ablating features is ineffective.
Intervening on multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
The specific decoder vectors are important for unlearning in gemma-2-2b-it, but not as critical in gemma-2b-it.
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, not the weights, so the original knowledge remains in the weights.
papers.limitation:
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, without modifying the model weights, so the original knowledge is still contained in the weights.
Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.
SAE-based unlearning results in similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
future_direction: Examine how SAE quality and width impact unlearning effectiveness.
Compare SAE-based unlearning to activation steering using bio-related and non-bio-related prompt pairs.
Investigate how SAE interventions affect related features in subsequent layers to better understand the unlearning mechanism.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models. We use the biology subset of the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy dataset and test on the gemma-2b-it and gemma-2-2b-it language models. We demonstrate that individual interpretable biology-related SAE features can be used to unlearn a subset of WMDP-Bio questions with minimal side-effects in domains other than biology. Our results suggest that negative scaling of feature activations is necessary and that zero ablating features is ineffective. We find that intervening using multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple different topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing Representation Misdirection for Unlearning technique. Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.

papers.title: Interpretable Steering of Large Language Models with Feature Guided Activation Additions
papers.research_question: How can we improve the precision and interpretability of activation steering in large language models by leveraging sparse autoencoder features and optimization techniques?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that uses sparse autoencoder features and optimization to construct precise, interpretable steering vectors, improving steering effectiveness and output coherence compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: FGAA represents a significant step forward in controlled text generation, offering both theoretical insights into activation patterns and practical advances in steering methodology, while highlighting the trade-off between steering strength and capability preservation.
papers.key_findings:
FGAA outperforms existing activation steering methods (CAA, SAE, SAE-TS) on most steering tasks, especially for the Gemma-2-2B model.
FGAA provides more interpretable steering by operating in the SAE feature space and allowing explicit control over which features are steered.
There is a trade-off between steering strength and preservation of model capabilities: all steering methods degrade model performance (perplexity and benchmark accuracy) at high steering scales.
Negative features in steering vectors tend to degrade steering performance, so FGAA focuses on positive features.
The effectiveness of FGAA varies with model size, showing different performance patterns between Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on the quality of feature extraction by the underlying Sparse Autoencoder (SAE).
Optimal selection of n1 and n2 parameters is task-dependent, making universal guidelines challenging.
Developing metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of feature filtering methods is challenging due to the qualitative nature of interpreting features.
future_direction: Investigating how SAE width and quality of SAE features affects steering performance with FGAA.
Exploring techniques to minimize capability degradation at higher steering scales while maintaining steering effectiveness.
Applying FGAA to safety tasks such as controlling sycophancy, hallucination, and refusal in RLHF models and reducing social biases.
papers.abstract: Effective and reliable control over large language model (LLM) behavior is a significant challenge. While activation steering methods, which add steering vectors to a model's hidden states, are a promising approach, existing techniques often lack precision and interpretability in how they influence model outputs. We introduce Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that leverages insights from Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS). By operating in the latent space of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and employing optimization techniques to select desired SAE features, FGAA constructs precise steering vectors that provide better steering effects while maintaining coherence of steered model outputs. In this regard, evaluations on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B models across various steering tasks demonstrate that FGAA outperforms existing steering methods of CAA, SAE decoder steering, and SAE-TS. Our results also highlight important trade-offs between steering scale and general model capabilities that are consistent across all tested steering methods.

papers.title: AudioSAE: Towards Understanding of Audio-Processing Models with Sparse AutoEncoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be effectively applied to audio-processing models to obtain stable, interpretable features, and do these features have practical utility?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces AudioSAE, applying sparse autoencoders to audio models (Whisper and HuBERT), demonstrating that they yield stable, interpretable features capturing acoustic and semantic information, and shows practical utility in hallucination reduction and correlation with human EEG.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are effective tools for interpreting audio-processing models, providing stable and interpretable features that have practical applications such as hallucination reduction and show alignment with human neural processing.
papers.key_findings:
Over 50% of SAE features remain consistent across random seeds.
SAE features capture general acoustic and semantic information as well as specific events like environmental noises and paralinguistic sounds.
Features disentangle concepts effectively, requiring removal of only 19–27% of features to erase a concept.
Feature steering reduces Whisper’s false speech detections by 70% with negligible WER increase.
SAE features are correlated with human EEG activity during speech perception, indicating alignment with human neural processing.
papers.limitation: The auto-interpretation method depends on empirically selected thresholds and is biased by the predominance of speech data in the test set, potentially obscuring rarer music or sound events, and is limited by the capabilities of the underlying audio captioning model.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are powerful tools for interpreting neural representations, yet their use in audio remains underexplored. We train SAEs across all encoder layers of Whisper and HuBERT, provide an extensive evaluation of their stability, interpretability, and show their practical utility. Over 50% of the features remain consistent across random seeds, and reconstruction quality is preserved. SAE features capture general acoustic and semantic information as well as specific events, including environmental noises and paralinguistic sounds (e.g. laughter, whispering) and disentangle them effectively, requiring removal of only 19-27% of features to erase a concept. Feature steering reduces Whisper's false speech detections by 70% with negligible WER increase, demonstrating real-world applicability. Finally, we find SAE features correlated with human EEG activity during speech perception, indicating alignment with human neural processing. The code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/audiosae/audiosae_demo.

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
papers.research_question: Does incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improve the reconstruction-interpretability frontier? Specifically, does it improve reconstruction, maintain or improve interpretability, and learn hierarchical semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (H-SAE) architecture that explicitly models semantic hierarchy, improving reconstruction performance and interpretability while being computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improves the reconstruction-interpretability frontier, leading to better reconstruction, maintained or improved interpretability, and learned hierarchical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
H-SAEs have better reconstruction performance than standard SAEs as measured by explained variance and downstream CE loss.
H-SAEs maintain or improve interpretability, showing less feature absorption and fewer redundant features across languages.
The H-SAE architecture learns hierarchical semantics, with high-level features capturing general concepts and low-level features capturing specific instances.
The hierarchical structure provides significant computational efficiency gains, allowing scaling to larger effective dictionary sizes with minimal overhead.
The architecture successfully translates theoretical insights about hierarchical concept geometry into a practical mixture-of-experts type model.
papers.limitation: Results are still imperfect, with some hard-to-interpret features and far from perfect reconstruction.
future_direction: Explore other reconstruction objectives beyond Euclidean distance.
Incorporate insights from causal representation learning into LLM interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.

papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: Training Superior Sparse Autoencoders for Instruct Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on instruct models, given that existing methods designed for base models result in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Finetuning-aligned Sequential Training (FAST), a novel method for training sparse autoencoders on instruct models that aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns of instruct models, leading to significant improvements in reconstruction quality and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: FAST is an effective method for training SAEs on instruct models, achieving superior reconstruction and feature interpretability, and the resulting SAEs can be used to steer model behavior via special token features, opening new avenues for model control.
papers.key_findings:
FAST significantly outperforms baseline Block Training methods (BT(P) and BT(F)) in token reconstruction (MSE) and special token reconstruction (MSEst) across multiple instruct models and SAE architectures.
FAST produces a higher proportion of high-quality, interpretable features compared to baseline methods, as measured by an automated feature interpretability scoring framework.
Intervening on the activations of special tokens via the trained SAEs can improve output quality and enable fine-grained control of model behavior, suggesting new applications for SAEs.
future_direction: Exploring the opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior through steering with SAE latents, particularly via special tokens.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow in scale and capability, understanding their internal mechanisms becomes increasingly critical. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a key tool in mechanistic interpretability, enabling the extraction of human-interpretable features from LLMs. However, existing SAE training methods are primarily designed for base models, resulting in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability when applied to instruct models. To bridge this gap, we propose $\underline{\textbf{F}}$inetuning-$\underline{\textbf{a}}$ligned $\underline{\textbf{S}}$equential $\underline{\textbf{T}}$raining ($\textit{FAST}$), a novel training method specifically tailored for instruct models. $\textit{FAST}$ aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns characteristic of instruct models, resulting in substantial improvements in both reconstruction and feature interpretability. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, $\textit{FAST}$ achieves a mean squared error of 0.6468 in token reconstruction, significantly outperforming baseline methods with errors of 5.1985 and 1.5096. In feature interpretability, $\textit{FAST}$ yields a higher proportion of high-quality features, for Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, $21.1\%$ scored in the top range, compared to $7.0\%$ and $10.2\%$ for $\textit{BT(P)}$ and $\textit{BT(F)}$. Surprisingly, we discover that intervening on the activations of special tokens via the SAEs leads to improvements in output quality, suggesting new opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior. Code, data, and 240 trained SAEs are available at https://github.com/Geaming2002/FAST.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
