papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How does the L0 hyperparameter (average number of active features per token) in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) affect the quality of learned features, and how can the correct L0 be determined?
papers.core_contribution: The L0 hyperparameter in Sparse Autoencoders must be set correctly to learn monosemantic features; if L0 is too low or too high, the SAE mixes correlated features, and the paper provides a proxy metric (decoder pairwise cosine similarity) to guide L0 selection.
papers.conclusion: The L0 hyperparameter must be set correctly for SAEs to learn correct, monosemantic features, and most existing SAEs likely have an L0 that is too low.
papers.key_findings:
If L0 is set too low, SAEs mix positively correlated features to improve reconstruction, leading to polysemantic latents.
If L0 is set too high, SAEs find degenerate solutions that also mix features.
Commonly used sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots are not a sound evaluation method, as they can favor incorrect SAEs that mix features over a ground-truth SAE.
A proxy metric, decoder pairwise cosine similarity (c_dec), is minimized when the SAE L0 matches the true underlying L0 of the data distribution.
Most commonly used open-source SAEs have an L0 that is too low.
papers.limitation:
The investigation is limited to features satisfying the linear representation hypothesis and does not consider non-linear underlying features.
The study only investigated a few layers of popular LLMs due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Investigate how SAEs react if the underlying features are non-linear.
Explore the impact of different correlation structures (e.g., unbalanced correlations) on SAEs.
Extend the analysis to more layers of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) extract features from LLM internal activations, meant to correspond to interpretable concepts. A core SAE training hyperparameter is L0: how many SAE features should fire per token on average. Existing work compares SAE algorithms using sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots, implying L0 is a free parameter with no single correct value aside from its effect on reconstruction. In this work we study the effect of L0 on SAEs, and show that if L0 is not set correctly, the SAE fails to disentangle the underlying features of the LLM. If L0 is too low, the SAE will mix correlated features to improve reconstruction. If L0 is too high, the SAE finds degenerate solutions that also mix features. Further, we present a proxy metric that can help guide the search for the correct L0 for an SAE on a given training distribution. We show that our method finds the correct L0 in toy models and coincides with peak sparse probing performance in LLM SAEs. We find that most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low. Our work shows that L0 must be set correctly to train SAEs with correct features.

papers.title: Which Sparse Autoencoder Features Are Real? Model-X Knockoffs for False Discovery Rate Control
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish real computational patterns from erroneous correlations in sparse autoencoder features? The paper investigates using Model-X knockoffs for false discovery rate control in SAE feature selection.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-X knockoffs for selecting sparse autoencoder features with false discovery rate control, revealing that only 25% of highly active SAE features encode genuine task-relevant information.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a rigorous statistical framework for identifying genuine SAE features with FDR control, addressing a critical gap in interpretability research and showing that naive feature analysis approaches are dominated by false positives.
papers.key_findings:
The method selected 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 from 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification.
Selected features show a 5.40× separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features.
Only about 25% of the examined latents carry task-relevant signal, while 75% do not.
A classifier using only the selected features achieved 77.4% training accuracy.
Features with negative knockoff statistics exist, indicating misleading patterns that would be selected by naive correlation-based approaches.
papers.limitation:
Feature reduction is necessary for stable covariance estimation (n > p), which may miss rare but important features.
Computational cost scales quadratically in p, becoming expensive for very large feature sets.
The method identifies which features are real but does not explain what those features represent.
The method identifies statistical association, not necessarily causal importance.
future_direction: Explore hierarchical testing strategies, approximate knockoff methods, or alternative covariance estimation techniques to handle p ≫ n settings.
Combine knockoff-based selection with automated interpretation pipelines to provide both statistical validation and conceptual understanding.
Investigate how feature validity varies across layers and tasks, and how selection interacts with different SAE training objectives and architectures.
papers.abstract: Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are crucial for identifying interpretable features in neural networks, it is still challenging to distinguish between real computational patterns and erroneous correlations. We introduce Model-X knockoffs to SAE feature selection, using knock-off+ to control the false discovery rate (FDR) with finite-sample guarantees under the standard Model-X assumptions (in our case, via a Gaussian surrogate for the latent distribution). We select 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 after analyzing 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification using Pythia-70M. About 25% of the latents under examination carry task-relevant signal, whereas 75% do not, according to the chosen set, which displays a 5.40x separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features. Our method offers a re-producible and principled framework for reliable feature discovery by combining SAEs with multiple-testing-aware inference, advancing the foundations of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) learn meaningful feature decompositions of neural network activations, or can their performance be matched by random baselines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) fail to reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms, as they recover very few ground-truth features in synthetic experiments and are matched in performance by simple random baselines on real model activations.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE evaluation practices are insufficient, and SAEs in their present state do not reliably learn meaningful feature decompositions. The proposed random baselines serve as simple sanity checks for future work.
papers.key_findings:
In synthetic experiments with known ground-truth features, SAEs recover only 9% of true features despite achieving 71% explained variance, showing a disconnect between reconstruction and feature recovery.
Three random baselines (Frozen Decoder, Soft-Frozen Decoder, Frozen Encoder) match fully-trained SAEs across key evaluation metrics: interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72).
In the synthetic variable probability setting, SAEs recover only the highest-frequency ground-truth features, leaving over 90% of the feature dictionary unmatched.
The reconstruction objective is a poor proxy for meaningful decomposition, as SAEs can achieve strong reconstruction without aligning with true features.
The competitive performance of frozen baselines suggests SAEs may operate in a 'lazy training' regime, achieving most gains through minimal adjustments to randomly initialized components.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic experiment assumes independent feature activations, omitting correlations that likely exist in real neural networks.
The work focuses on standard SAE architectures and does not evaluate related approaches such as transcoders or crosscoders.
future_direction: Explore objectives that more directly incentivize feature alignment rather than just reconstruction.
Design appropriate randomization baselines for related methods like transcoders and crosscoders.
Incorporate more realistic feature dependencies in synthetic evaluation setups.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for interpreting neural networks by decomposing their activations into sparse sets of human-interpretable features. Recent work has introduced multiple SAE variants and successfully scaled them to frontier models. Despite much excitement, a growing number of negative results in downstream tasks casts doubt on whether SAEs recover meaningful features. To directly investigate this, we perform two complementary evaluations. On a synthetic setup with known ground-truth features, we demonstrate that SAEs recover only $9\%$ of true features despite achieving $71\%$ explained variance, showing that they fail at their core task even when reconstruction is strong. To evaluate SAEs on real activations, we introduce three baselines that constrain SAE feature directions or their activation patterns to random values. Through extensive experiments across multiple SAE architectures, we show that our baselines match fully-trained SAEs in interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72). Together, these results suggest that SAEs in their current state do not reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: Feature-Level Insights into Artificial Text Detection with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders be used to improve interpretability in Artificial Text Detection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can extract interpretable features from LLM residual streams for artificial text detection, revealing distinct writing styles in AI-generated text.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Sparse Autoencoder-based analysis is a valuable tool for understanding text generators and detectors, highlighting that AI-generated text detection is easy with default prompts but challenging with style changes.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-derived features outperform raw activations in detecting artificial text across various datasets.
General features (e.g., 3608, 4645) are effective across multiple domains and models for ATD.
Domain-specific features (e.g., for arXiv, finance) capture stylistic variations in AI-generated text.
Modern LLMs have detectable writing styles, such as excessive complexity and repetition, but can produce human-like text with personalized prompts.
Feature steering and interpretation provide insights into how features affect text generation.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty in predicting performance on future LLMs and novel attack strategies.
Only a subset of attacks are covered.
Some SAE features remain challenging to interpret.
Using only one SAE on the residual stream of Gemma 2-2B limits generalizability.
future_direction: Exploring different SAEs on other LLMs for additional insights.
papers.abstract: Artificial Text Detection (ATD) is becoming increasingly important with the rise of advanced Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite numerous efforts, no single algorithm performs consistently well across different types of unseen text or guarantees effective generalization to new LLMs. Interpretability plays a crucial role in achieving this goal. In this study, we enhance ATD interpretability by using Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) to extract features from Gemma-2-2b residual stream. We identify both interpretable and efficient features, analyzing their semantics and relevance through domain- and model-specific statistics, a steering approach, and manual or LLM-based interpretation. Our methods offer valuable insights into how texts from various models differ from human-written content. We show that modern LLMs have a distinct writing style, especially in information-dense domains, even though they can produce human-like outputs with personalized prompts.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Temporal Difference Learning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models implement temporal difference learning to solve reinforcement learning problems in-context, despite being trained only for next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders can reveal and causally manipulate these representations.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders provide a methodology for studying and manipulating these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 3 70B can solve simple reinforcement learning problems in-context and its behavior is best described by a Q-learning model.
Sparse autoencoders trained on the residual stream reveal features that correlate with temporal difference errors and Q-values.
Intervening on these temporal difference features (lesioning or clamping) impairs performance and reduces correlations, demonstrating their causal involvement.
In a grid world task, Llama uses temporal difference-like features to predict the actions of a Q-learning agent.
In a graph learning task, Llama learns global graph structure similarly to the successor representation, and temporal difference features support this learning.
papers.limitation:
The sparse autoencoders are task-specific and not suitable for identifying reinforcement learning variables for arbitrary tasks.
A circuit-level understanding of how these representations come about remains unclear.
The alignment between the model's behavior and the Q-learning agent is not perfect.
future_direction: Build more generic sparse autoencoders for arbitrary tasks.
Replicate findings with different large language models.
Achieve a circuit-level understanding of how temporal difference representations are computed.
Extend the Q-learning model to account for repetition tendencies.
papers.abstract: In-context learning, the ability to adapt based on a few examples in the input prompt, is a ubiquitous feature of large language models (LLMs). However, as LLMs' in-context learning abilities continue to improve, understanding this phenomenon mechanistically becomes increasingly important. In particular, it is not well-understood how LLMs learn to solve specific classes of problems, such as reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in-context. Through three different tasks, we first show that Llama $3$ $70$B can solve simple RL problems in-context. We then analyze the residual stream of Llama using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and find representations that closely match temporal difference (TD) errors. Notably, these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token. We verify that these representations are indeed causally involved in the computation of TD errors and $Q$-values by performing carefully designed interventions on them. Taken together, our work establishes a methodology for studying and manipulating in-context learning with SAEs, paving the way for a more mechanistic understanding.

papers.title: CorrSteer: Generation-Time LLM Steering via Correlated Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we effectively steer large language models using Sparse Autoencoder features without requiring contrastive datasets or large activation storage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CorrSteer, a fully automated pipeline that selects task-relevant Sparse Autoencoder features by correlating generation-time activations with task outcomes, and uses these features to steer model behavior with reduced side effects.
papers.conclusion: CorrSteer establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across diverse language model applications.
papers.key_findings:
CorrSteer improves performance on QA, bias mitigation, and safety benchmarks, e.g., +3.3% on MMLU and +27.2% on HarmBench.
Correlation-based feature selection is effective and scalable, requiring only inference-time activations and no contrastive data.
Multi-layer steering (CorrSteer-A, CorrSteer-P) outperforms single-feature steering, suggesting collaborative circuit effects.
CorrSteer reduces side effects compared to fine-tuning, as measured by the Side Effect Ratio (SER).
Selected features are semantically interpretable and align with task requirements (e.g., refusal features for safety, structured output for multiple-choice).
papers.limitation:
CorrSteer is static and cannot easily adapt to dynamic tasks or separate benign from harmful requests without additional context.
The method may capture spurious correlations rather than causal relationships, especially with limited samples.
future_direction: Extend CorrSteer to dynamic tasks and sequential decision-making.
Improve feature selection to further reduce spurious correlations.
Apply the method to larger models and more complex domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable features from large language models (LLMs) without supervision. However, their effectiveness in downstream steering tasks is limited by the requirement for contrastive datasets or large activation storage. To address these limitations, we propose CorrSteer, which selects features by correlating sample correctness with SAE activations from generated tokens at inference time. This approach uses only inference-time activations to extract more relevant features, thereby reducing spurious correlations. It also obtains steering coefficients from average activations, automating the entire pipeline. Our method shows improved task performance on QA, bias mitigation, jailbreaking prevention, and reasoning benchmarks on Gemma-2 2B and LLaMA-3.1 8B, notably achieving a +3.3% improvement in MMLU performance with 4000 samples and a +27.2% improvement in HarmBench with only 108 samples. Selected features demonstrate semantically meaningful patterns aligned with each task's requirements, revealing the underlying capabilities that drive performance. Our work establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across language model applications.

papers.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders scale to large models like Claude 3 Sonnet to extract interpretable features, and what do these features reveal about model behavior and safety?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can be scaled to extract interpretable, abstract features from Claude 3 Sonnet, revealing safety-relevant concepts and enabling model steering.
papers.conclusion: The method successfully scales to large models, providing insights into model internals and potential tools for safety, but further research is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders produce interpretable features for large models like Claude 3 Sonnet.
Scaling laws can guide the training of sparse autoencoders to optimize feature extraction.
Extracted features are highly abstract, multilingual, and multimodal.
Features can be used to steer model behavior, demonstrating causal influence.
Safety-relevant features related to bias, deception, sycophancy, and dangerous content are discovered.
papers.limitation:
The research is preliminary and caution is needed in interpreting safety-relevant features.
Sparse autoencoders have dead features and may not capture all concepts.
future_direction: Further work to understand the implications of safety-relevant features.
Improving sparse autoencoder training to reduce dead features.
Rigorous comparison of feature-based steering with other methods.
papers.abstract: Can sparse autoencoders scale to large models like Claude 3 Sonnet to extract interpretable features, and what do these features reveal about model behavior and safety? Sparse autoencoders can be scaled to extract interpretable, abstract features from Claude 3 Sonnet, revealing safety-relevant concepts and enabling model steering. The method successfully scales to large models, providing insights into model internals and potential tools for safety, but further research is needed.

papers.title: Transferring Linear Features Across Language Models With Model Stitching
papers.research_question: Can linear features (e.g., from Sparse Autoencoders, probes, and steering vectors) be transferred between language models of different sizes using affine mappings (model stitching), and what are the implications for efficiency and feature universality?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that affine mappings (stitches) between residual streams can effectively transfer linear features across language models, enabling compute-efficient training of Sparse Autoencoders and transfer of probes and steering vectors, while revealing differences in how semantic and structural features transfer.
papers.conclusion: Linear features can be transferred between language models via affine mappings, supporting weak universality and providing a method to improve the training efficiency of interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Using transferred SAEs as initialization can reduce FLOPs by ~50% when training SAEs on larger models.
Probes and steering vectors can be transferred between models with no additional training in specific cases (e.g., language steering).
Structural features (syntactic) transfer more consistently than semantic features, which are more polarized in transferability.
Specific functional features (e.g., entropy and attention deactivation features) preserve their roles after transfer.
Linear stitches support a weak universality hypothesis, showing that small and large models learn similar representation spaces.
papers.limitation:
Stitches are only trained on general internet text between models in the same family with the same tokenizer.
The scaling law analysis is theoretically incomplete due to lack of high-compute regime data to fit the irreducible loss.
The semantic/structural classification is imperfect and noisy due to reliance on another LLM for augmentations.
Probing and steering experiments are limited to particular tasks and settings.
future_direction: Verify findings in cross-family model settings and finetune stitches on special tokens or chat-templated data.
Explore other applications of stitches, such as transferring linear weight updates like LoRAs.
Expand probing and steering experiments to examine robustness and broader task settings.
papers.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that affine mappings between residual streams of language models is a cheap way to effectively transfer represented features between models. We apply this technique to transfer the weights of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) between models of different sizes to compare their representations. We find that small and large models learn similar representation spaces, which motivates training expensive components like SAEs on a smaller model and transferring to a larger model at a FLOPs savings. In particular, using a small-to-large transferred SAE as initialization can lead to 50% cheaper training runs when training SAEs on larger models. Next, we show that transferred probes and steering vectors can effectively recover ground truth performance. Finally, we dive deeper into feature-level transferability, finding that semantic and structural features transfer noticeably differently while specific classes of functional features have their roles faithfully mapped. Overall, our findings illustrate similarities and differences in the linear representation spaces of small and large models and demonstrate a method for improving the training efficiency of SAEs.

papers.title: One-Step is Enough: Sparse Autoencoders for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders learn interpretable features for text-to-image diffusion models, and do these features generalize across different denoising steps and model architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs can learn interpretable features from one-step text-to-image diffusion models that generalize across steps and architectures, enabling causal intervention and revealing block specialization.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image diffusion models, and one-step training is sufficient for learning features that generalize to multi-step models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on one-step SDXL Turbo generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and multi-step SDXL base model without additional training.
The learned features are interpretable and causally influence the image generation process.
Transformer blocks specialize into roles: up.0.0 for details, up.0.1 for style, and down.2.1 for composition.
RIEBench shows SAE features allow fine-grained image editing with fewer features compared to neuron interventions.
One-step training is sufficient for learning meaningful features applicable to multi-step diffusion models.
papers.limitation: The change pose task is hard to achieve with the current RIEBench setup.
future_direction: Improving feature selection strategies for delete interventions
Extending SAEs to other diffusion models
Using learned features for advanced image editing and control
papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs), sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been shown to decompose intermediate representations that often are not interpretable directly into sparse sums of interpretable features, facilitating better control and subsequent analysis. However, similar analyses and approaches have been lacking for text-to-image models. We investigate the possibility of using SAEs to learn interpretable features for SDXL Turbo, a few-step text-to-image diffusion model. To this end, we train SAEs on the updates performed by transformer blocks within SDXL Turbo's denoising U-net in its 1-step setting. Interestingly, we find that they generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and even to the multi-step SDXL base model (i.e., a different model) without additional training. In addition, we show that their learned features are interpretable, causally influence the generation process, and reveal specialization among the blocks. We do so by creating RIEBench, a representation-based image editing benchmark, for editing images while they are generated by turning on and off individual SAE features. This allows us to track which transformer blocks' features are the most impactful depending on the edit category. Our work is the first investigation of SAEs for interpretability in text-to-image diffusion models and our results establish SAEs as a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image models.

papers.title: Exploring Task Performance with Interpretable Models via Sparse Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: We investigated the extent to which the decomposition of traditionally black-box LLMs can aid in increasing their interpretability and lead to performance improvements in downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to decompose LLMs, identify model-internal misunderstandings, and automatically reformulate prompts to improve performance on downstream tasks like mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection.
papers.conclusion: Decomposing LLMs with dictionary learning and sparse autoencoders improves interpretability and leads to performance gains in mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection by identifying and correcting model-internal misunderstandings.
papers.key_findings:
Decomposing LLMs with sparse autoencoders allows identification of ambiguous mathematical symbols and metaphorical terms.
Automatic reformulation of prompts based on identified ambiguities improves accuracy in mathematical reasoning across multiple models and domains.
The method also improves metaphor detection accuracy, outperforming previous task-specific models.
The improvements are statistically significant, as shown by paired t-tests.
The framework is model-agnostic and works across different LLMs (Llama 3, Mistral, Gemma, Phi-3).
papers.limitation:
The work does not introduce a new interpretability technique but applies existing techniques in a novel framework.
The approach is only tested on two downstream tasks (mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection), and performance on other tasks may vary.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are traditionally viewed as black-box algorithms, therefore reducing trustworthiness and obscuring potential approaches to increasing performance on downstream tasks. In this work, we apply an effective LLM decomposition method using a dictionary-learning approach with sparse autoencoders. This helps extract monosemantic features from polysemantic LLM neurons. Remarkably, our work identifies model-internal misunderstanding, allowing the automatic reformulation of the prompts with additional annotations to improve the interpretation by LLMs. Moreover, this approach demonstrates a significant performance improvement in downstream tasks, such as mathematical reasoning and metaphor detection.

papers.title: The Knowledge Microscope: Features as Better Analytical Lenses than Neurons
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether features (obtained via Sparse Autoencoders) are better analytical units than neurons for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in language models, addressing challenges of limited knowledge expression, poor interpretability, polysemanticity, and performance in downstream tasks like privacy erasure.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that features extracted via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are superior analytical units to neurons for studying factual knowledge in language models, exhibiting stronger impact on knowledge expression, better interpretability, stronger monosemanticity, and enabling more effective privacy erasure through the proposed FeatureEdit method.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that features are better analytical units than neurons for understanding factual knowledge in language models, and the proposed FeatureEdit method effectively leverages features for privacy erasure.
papers.key_findings:
SAE is effective in decomposing neurons into features for studying factual knowledge mechanisms.
Features, especially post-MLP features, have a stronger impact on knowledge expression than neurons.
Features demonstrate superior interpretability compared to neurons.
Features exhibit stronger monosemanticity, with clear activation patterns for related facts and inactivity for unrelated ones.
The proposed feature-based editing method, FeatureEdit, outperforms neuron-based methods in erasing privacy-sensitive knowledge while maintaining better generalization and causing less damage to general model capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mapping from features back to weights is indirect and sub-optimal, requiring reconstruction.
The clustering phenomenon of SAE features and their stability across different numbers of features require further investigation.
future_direction: Investigate the inherent stable structure of SAE feature space and whether it is truly insensitive to the number of features.
Improve the mapping from features back to weights for more direct model editing.
papers.abstract: Previous studies primarily utilize MLP neurons as units of analysis for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in Language Models (LMs); however, neurons suffer from polysemanticity, leading to limited knowledge expression and poor interpretability. In this paper, we first conduct preliminary experiments to validate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) can effectively decompose neurons into features, which serve as alternative analytical units. With this established, our core findings reveal three key advantages of features over neurons: (1) Features exhibit stronger influence on knowledge expression and superior interpretability. (2) Features demonstrate enhanced monosemanticity, showing distinct activation patterns between related and unrelated facts. (3) Features achieve better privacy protection than neurons, demonstrated through our proposed FeatureEdit method, which significantly outperforms existing neuron-based approaches in erasing privacy-sensitive information from LMs.Code and dataset will be available.

papers.title: Decomposing MLP Activations into Interpretable Features via Semi-Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
papers.research_question: How can we find interpretable features in large language models by decomposing MLP activations using semi-nonnegative matrix factorization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SNMF for decomposing MLP activations into interpretable features, outperforming SAEs and supervised baselines in causal steering, and reveals hierarchical structure in MLP activation space.
papers.conclusion: SNMF is a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SNMF-derived features outperform SAEs and a supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering.
SNMF features align with human-interpretable concepts and show good concept detection.
Recursive SNMF reveals hierarchical merging of features, e.g., fine-grained concepts into high-level ones.
Specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features.
MLP features are compositional and exhibit a parts-based decomposition.
papers.limitation: A minority of MLP features receive negative scores, indicating they respond more strongly to neutral contexts, possibly reflecting sensitivity to noise or layer-specific biases.
future_direction: Optimizations for SNMF initialization and training
papers.abstract: A central goal for mechanistic interpretability has been to identify the right units of analysis in large language models (LLMs) that causally explain their outputs. While early work focused on individual neurons, evidence that neurons often encode multiple concepts has motivated a shift toward analyzing directions in activation space. A key question is how to find directions that capture interpretable features in an unsupervised manner. Current methods rely on dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), commonly trained over residual stream activations to learn directions from scratch. However, SAEs often struggle in causal evaluations and lack intrinsic interpretability, as their learning is not explicitly tied to the computations of the model. Here, we tackle these limitations by directly decomposing MLP activations with semi-nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF), such that the learned features are (a) sparse linear combinations of co-activated neurons, and (b) mapped to their activating inputs, making them directly interpretable. Experiments on Llama 3.1, Gemma 2 and GPT-2 show that SNMF derived features outperform SAEs and a strong supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering, while aligning with human-interpretable concepts. Further analysis reveals that specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features, exposing a hierarchical structure in the MLP's activation space. Together, these results position SNMF as a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.

papers.title: Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the structure of SAE error (dark matter)? Can SAE error be predicted from activations? How do the linearly predictable and nonlinearly predictable components differ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that SAE error (dark matter) is largely linearly predictable from model activations, and that the nonlinear component is qualitatively different, containing fewer not-yet-learned features and being harder to learn.
papers.conclusion: The fact that SAE error can be predicted and analyzed is surprising, indicating SAE errors are worthy of analysis. The presence of constant nonlinear error at fixed sparsity suggests scaling SAEs may not be the only way to explain more of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAE error norms and vectors can be linearly predicted from activations with high accuracy (R2 between 70-95% for norms, 15-72% for vectors).
The scaling behavior of SAE error norms is predictable across different SAE sizes; larger SAEs struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs.
The nonlinear component of SAE error contains fewer not-yet-learned features, is harder to learn SAEs for, and contributes proportionally to cross entropy loss.
Inference time gradient pursuit reduces total FVU by 3-5% but leaves nonlinear error mostly unchanged.
Linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs can reduce nonlinear error and total SAE error.
future_direction: Explore alternative penalties besides sparsity or new ways to learn better dictionaries.
Incorporate low-rank dense side channels in SAE architecture.
Use small-scale trials to forecast SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising technique for decomposing language model activations into interpretable linear features. However, current SAEs fall short of completely explaining model performance, resulting in "dark matter": unexplained variance in activations. This work investigates dark matter as an object of study in its own right. Surprisingly, we find that much of SAE dark matter -- about half of the error vector itself and >90% of its norm -- can be linearly predicted from the initial activation vector. Additionally, we find that the scaling behavior of SAE error norms at a per token level is remarkably predictable: larger SAEs mostly struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs. We build on the linear representation hypothesis to propose models of activations that might lead to these observations. These insights imply that the part of the SAE error vector that cannot be linearly predicted ("nonlinear" error) might be fundamentally different from the linearly predictable component. To validate this hypothesis, we empirically analyze nonlinear SAE error and show that 1) it contains fewer not yet learned features, 2) SAEs trained on it are quantitatively worse, and 3) it is responsible for a proportional amount of the downstream increase in cross entropy loss when SAE activations are inserted into the model. Finally, we examine two methods to reduce nonlinear SAE error: inference time gradient pursuit, which leads to a very slight decrease in nonlinear error, and linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs, which leads to a larger reduction.

papers.title: Features that Make a Difference: Leveraging Gradients for Improved Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be improved to learn features that are more causally relevant to model outputs by incorporating gradient information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gradient SAEs (g-SAEs), which modify the TopK activation function in sparse autoencoders to incorporate gradient information, resulting in latents that are more causally relevant and better for steering model outputs without sacrificing interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating gradient information into SAEs improves their ability to capture causally relevant features and enhances steerability without compromising interpretability, advancing dictionary learning towards accounting for both representational and causal aspects of model features.
papers.key_findings:
g-SAEs produce reconstructions that are more faithful to original network performance for a given sparsity level.
g-SAEs learn latents that are more effective at steering models in arbitrary contexts, increasing the probability of associated tokens more strongly and specifically.
g-SAEs have fewer permanently inactive ('dead') latents compared to other SAE architectures.
g-SAEs show improved performance (lower loss added) across different model sizes (GPT-2 small to xl).
g-SAEs do not sacrifice interpretability, as human evaluators rate them similarly to standard TopK SAEs.
papers.limitation:
Activation plateaus: models may be robust to small perturbations, so gradients might not capture sensitivity to larger perturbations.
Computational complexity: g-SAEs require backpropagation, though in practice it was not a bottleneck.
Evaluations: need for more thorough evaluations and understanding of how token-level steerability translates to higher levels of abstraction.
future_direction: Investigating how to incorporate higher-order derivative information to address activation plateaus.
Developing more comprehensive evaluation frameworks for SAEs.
Studying how increased steerability on the token level translates to higher levels of abstraction.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach for extracting neural network features by learning a sparse and overcomplete decomposition of the network's internal activations.However, SAEs are traditionally trained considering only activation values and not the effect those activations have on downstream computations.This limits the information available to learn features, and biases the autoencoder towards neglecting features which are represented with small activation values but strongly influence model outputs.To address this, we introduce Gradient SAEs (g-SAEs), which modify the k-sparse autoencoder architecture by augmenting the TopK activation function to rely on the gradients of the input activation when selecting the k elements.For a given sparsity level, g-SAEs produce reconstructions that are more faithful to original network performance when propagated through the network.Additionally, we find evidence that g-SAEs learn latents that are on average more effective at steering models in arbitrary contexts.By considering the downstream effects of activations, our approach leverages the dual nature of neural network features as both representations, retrospectively, and actions, prospectively.While previous methods have approached the problem of feature discovery primarily focused on the former aspect, g-SAEs represent a step towards accounting for the latter as well.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model behavior in a more interpretable and fine-grained way by leveraging sparse representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Steering (SAS), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable steering vectors from contrastive prompt pairs, enabling precise and modular control over LLM behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SAS provides an effective framework for steering LLM behavior in sparse spaces, offering improved interpretability and fine-grained control compared to dense activation steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control over LLM outputs.
Scaling sparse autoencoders (increasing dictionary size) improves the monosemanticity of the extracted SAS vectors.
Sparse representations allow for modular control, enabling fine-grained behaviors to be composed simultaneously.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in AI alignment is guiding large language models (LLMs) to follow desired behaviors at test time. Activation steering, which modifies internal model activations during inference, offers a potential solution. However, prior work in dense activation spaces struggles with superposition, wherein multiple features become entangled, limiting interpretability and precise control. In contrast, sparse representations provide an untapped opportunity for more interpretable behavior modulation. In this work, we introduce sparse activation steering (SAS), a method that leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steer LLM behavior in sparse spaces. By isolating behavior-specific features through a contrastive prompt-pairing approach, we define a set of features that can selectively reinforce or suppress behaviors. Experiments on Gemma 2 LLMs show that SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control. Furthermore, scaling SAEs improves monosemanticity of SAS vectors, suggesting more reliable and interpretable interventions.

papers.title: Enhancing LLM Steering through Sparse Autoencoder-Based Vector Refinement
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors for controlling large language models be refined to be effective when only limited training data is available?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-RSV, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to semantically denoise and augment steering vectors learned from limited data, improving steering performance without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: SAE-RSV is an efficient and interpretable approach for enhancing the steering performance of LLMs with limited training data.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-RSV consistently outperforms all baseline methods, including supervised fine-tuning, across five behavioral concept datasets.
Both the denoising module (removing task-irrelevant features) and the augmentation module (adding missing task-relevant features) contribute to improved steering performance.
Optimal steering performance is achieved with around 15-20 task-relevant features; using too few or too many features degrades performance.
The method is robust to variations in training data size, performing well even with only 10 samples.
The semantics of the selected features align well with the target steering behavior, validating the feature selection approach.
papers.abstract: Steering has emerged as a promising approach in controlling large language models (LLMs) without modifying model parameters. However, most existing steering methods rely on large-scale datasets to learn clear behavioral information, which limits their applicability in many real-world scenarios. The steering vectors extracted from small dataset often contain task-irrelevant noising features, which degrades their effectiveness. To refine the steering vectors learned from limited data, we introduce Refinement of Steering Vector via Sparse Autoencoder (SAE-RSV) that leverages SAEs to semantically denoise and augment the steering vectors. In our framework, we first remove task-irrelevant features according to their semantics provided by SAEs, and then enrich task-relevant features missing from the small dataset through their semantic similarity to the identified relevant features. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SAE-RSV substantially outperforms all the baseline methods including supervised fine-tuning. Our findings show that effective steering vector can be constructed from limited training data by refining the original steering vector through SAEs.

papers.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to interpret the internal representations of a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model (MAIRA-2) and steer its generations?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology MLLM MAIRA-2, identifying a subset of interpretable clinical concepts within its representations and demonstrating the feasibility and challenges of steering model generations using these features.
papers.conclusion: The study provides initial insights into the internal concepts of MAIRA-2 using SAEs, marking a step toward mechanistic interpretability, while highlighting practical and methodological challenges in automated interpretability and steering.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset (1.8%) of SAE features are highly interpretable (F1 > 0.75), corresponding to clinically relevant concepts like medical devices, pathologies, and textual features.
Nearly half (46%) of SAE features are not interpretable by the automated pipeline (F1 < 0.5).
Steering model generations using SAE features is possible but produces more off-target changes than on-target changes, with success highly dependent on the specific feature.
There is a strong correlation between the on-target effects of positive and negative steering coefficients.
The trained SAEs and their automated interpretations are publicly released to foster further research.
papers.limitation:
Many SAE features (46%) are not interpretable by the automated pipeline.
Steering often produces more off-target changes than on-target changes.
The study reveals practical and methodological challenges across the SAE training, automated concept discovery, and steering pipeline.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can improve the safety, transparency and trust of AI models, which is especially important in healthcare applications where decisions often carry significant consequences. Mechanistic interpretability, particularly through the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs), offers a promising approach for uncovering human-interpretable features within large transformer-based models. In this study, we apply Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology-specialised multimodal large language model, MAIRA-2, to interpret its internal representations. Using large-scale automated interpretability of the SAE features, we identify a range of clinically relevant concepts - including medical devices (e.g., line and tube placements, pacemaker presence), pathologies such as pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, longitudinal changes and textual features. We further examine the influence of these features on model behaviour through steering, demonstrating directional control over generations with mixed success. Our results reveal practical and methodological challenges, yet they offer initial insights into the internal concepts learned by MAIRA-2 - marking a step toward deeper mechanistic understanding and interpretability of a radiology-adapted multimodal large language model, and paving the way for improved model transparency. We release the trained SAEs and interpretations: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/maira-2-sae.

papers.title: TopK Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we build a language model architecture that enjoys the interpretability of sparse autoencoders without suffering the drawbacks of post-hoc training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TopK LMs, a transformer-based language model architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function to achieve inherent, SAE-like interpretability without requiring post-hoc training, while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: TopK LMs represent a significant advance toward trustworthy AI systems by making interpretability a built-in feature, demonstrating that performance and interpretability need not be competing objectives.
papers.key_findings:
TopK LMs achieve competitive language modeling and downstream task performance compared to dense baselines, with only a moderate increase in model size.
Neurons in TopK LMs exhibit higher concept specialization, as measured by lower token and semantic entropy, making them more interpretable.
Single-neuron interventions (activation patching) can causally steer the model's text generation towards specific concepts.
The formation and specialization of individual neurons can be traced continuously across training checkpoints and model layers.
Sparsity annealing during training improves convergence and model performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models up to ~1B parameters; effectiveness on significantly larger models remains an open question.
Evaluation focused on language modeling and standard reasoning benchmarks, leaving performance on specialized downstream tasks unclear.
Long-context modeling capabilities and the interaction between TopK sparsity and attention over long sequences were not examined.
The approach is currently limited to text-only models; extending to multimodal architectures requires future research.
Specific societal applications that could benefit from the model's interpretability were not explored.
future_direction: Scaling the TopK LM approach to significantly larger models (tens or hundreds of billions of parameters).
Extending TopK activation to multimodal architectures combining text with images, audio, or other modalities.
Investigating how TopK LMs can address concrete challenges in model alignment, fairness assessment, safety evaluation, and trustworthy AI deployment.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for analyzing and interpreting the activation space of transformer-based language models (LMs). However, SAEs suffer several shortcomings that diminish their utility and internal validity. Since SAEs are trained post-hoc, it is unclear if the failure to discover a particular concept is a failure on the SAE's side or due to the underlying LM not representing this concept. This problem is exacerbated by training conditions and architecture choices affecting which features an SAE learns. When tracing how LMs learn concepts during training, the lack of feature stability also makes it difficult to compare SAEs features across different checkpoints. To address these limitations, we introduce a modification to the transformer architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function at chosen layers, making the model's hidden states equivalent to the latent features of a TopK SAE. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc training while providing interpretability comparable to SAEs. The resulting TopK LMs offer a favorable trade-off between model size, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Despite this simple architectural change, TopK LMs maintain their original capabilities while providing robust interpretability benefits. Our experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations learned by TopK LMs enable successful steering through targeted neuron interventions and facilitate detailed analysis of neuron formation processes across checkpoints and layers. These features make TopK LMs stable and reliable tools for understanding how language models learn and represent concepts, which we believe will significantly advance future research on model interpretability and controllability.

papers.title: Attention Layers Add Into Low-Dimensional Residual Subspaces
papers.research_question: What causes dead features in sparse dictionary learning for attention outputs, and how can we mitigate this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that attention outputs in transformers have a low-rank structure, which causes dead features in sparse dictionary learning. It proposes Active Subspace Initialization for SAEs to align features with the active subspace, drastically reducing dead features.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide new insights into the geometry of attention and practical tools for improving sparse dictionary learning in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Attention outputs have low effective rank (~60%) compared to MLP outputs and residual streams (~90%).
This low-rank structure is consistent across layers, models, and datasets.
The low-rank structure is primarily due to the output projection matrix W_O.
Low effective rank strongly correlates with dead features in SAEs.
Active Subspace Initialization reduces dead features from 87% to below 1% in large SAEs and improves reconstruction.
papers.limitation: Some dead features remain at extremely large scales in Active Subspace Initialization.
future_direction: Extend Active Subspace Initialization to transcoders and cross-layer transcoders for MLP replacements.
papers.abstract: Transformer architectures, and their attention mechanisms in particular, form the foundation of modern large language models. While transformer models are widely believed to operate in high-dimensional hidden spaces, we show that attention outputs are confined to a surprisingly low-dimensional subspace, where about 60\% of the directions account for 99\% of the variance--a phenomenon that is consistently observed across diverse model families and datasets, and is induced by the attention output projection matrix. Critically, we find this low-rank structure as a key factor of the prevalent dead feature problem in sparse dictionary learning, where it creates a mismatch between randomly initialized features and the intrinsic geometry of the activation space. Building on this insight, we propose a subspace-constrained training method for sparse autoencoders (SAEs), initializing feature directions into the active subspace of activations. Our approach reduces dead features from 87\% to below 1\% in Attention Output SAEs with 1M features, and can further extend to other sparse dictionary learning methods. Our findings provide both new insights into the geometry of attention and practical tools for improving sparse dictionary learning in large language models.

papers.title: The Missing Curve Detectors of InceptionV1: Applying Sparse Autoencoders to InceptionV1 Early Vision
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features and address polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1's early vision layers?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable features from InceptionV1, revealing missing curve detectors and decomposing polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic features.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1 and convolutional neural networks, extending their promise beyond language models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn new interpretable features that were not visible when examining individual neurons.
SAEs discover additional curve detector features that fill gaps in the known family of curve detectors.
SAEs can split polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features.
papers.limitation: This paper is a very early report and does not defend the results in a systematic way.
future_direction: Investigate branch specialization and cross-branch superposition in InceptionV1 using SAEs.
papers.abstract: Recent work on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has shown promise in extracting interpretable features from neural networks and addressing challenges with polysemantic neurons caused by superposition. In this paper, we apply SAEs to the early vision layers of InceptionV1, a well-studied convolutional neural network, with a focus on curve detectors. Our results demonstrate that SAEs can uncover new interpretable features not apparent from examining individual neurons, including additional curve detectors that fill in previous gaps. We also find that SAEs can decompose some polysemantic neurons into more monosemantic constituent features. These findings suggest SAEs are a valuable tool for understanding InceptionV1, and convolutional neural networks more generally.

papers.title: Interpretable LLM Guardrails via Sparse Representation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior to mitigate harmful, misleading, or biased content using sparse representation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SRS, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to disentangle activations into monosemantic features and steer LLM behavior via sparse steering vectors, achieving fine-grained control while preserving output quality.
papers.conclusion: SRS enables precise and interpretable steering of LLM behavior using sparse representations, providing a reliable guardrail for safety, fairness, and truthfulness with superior performance over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRS outperforms existing steering methods like CAA and SAE-TS in single-attribute and multi-attribute control tasks.
SRS maintains high linguistic quality, including grammatical correctness and language diversity, with minimal side effects.
SRS demonstrates robustness against diverse jailbreak prompts, achieving high defense rates.
Multi-attribute control with PCA composition strategy yields the best trade-off between control effectiveness and content quality.
Sparse features enable interpretable identification of attribute-relevant dimensions through KL divergence analysis.
papers.limitation: Multi-attribute steering strategies such as PCA may not fully capture complex relationships and conflicts between attributes.
future_direction: Layer-wise or component-wise multi-attribute steering to align interventions with semantic levels.
Context-aware and personalized steering based on semantic subdomains of prompts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities in generation tasks but are prone to producing harmful, misleading, or biased content, posing significant ethical and safety concerns. To mitigate such risks, representation engineering, which steer model behavior toward desired attributes by injecting carefully designed steering vectors into LLM's representations at inference time, has emerged as a promising alternative to fine-tuning approaches. However, due to the semantically entangled nature of LLM's representation, existing representation engineering methods still suffer from several limitations: limited fine-grained controllability, content quality degradation, and conflict in multi-attribute control. To overcome these challenges, we propose Sparse Representation Steering (SRS), a novel framework that achieves fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior by first disentangling internal activations into a sparse, semantically meaningful representation space, and then selectively steering relevant dimensions. Specifically, SRS leverages a pretrained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to transform dense, entangled activation patterns into a sparse monosemantic feature space. To identify relevant features, SRS contrasts sparse activations from positive and negative prompt pairs and measures their bidirectional KL divergence to locate dimensions most associated with the target attribute. We conduct comprehensive experiments on Gemma-2 series model across three alignment dimensions, i.e., safety, fairness, and truthfulness, to evaluate the effectiveness of SRS. Results show that SRS consistently outperforms existing steering methods, which achieves significantly improved controllability across both single and multiple attribute settings, while preserving high linguistic quality and general ability.

papers.title: Learning Interpretable Features in Audio Latent Spaces via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we interpret audio generative models by mapping their latent representations to human-interpretable acoustic concepts, given the challenges of audio's dense nature and limited automatic feature characterization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for interpreting audio generative models by training sparse autoencoders on their latent spaces and learning linear mappings from SAE features to discretized acoustic properties (pitch, amplitude, timbre), enabling both controllable manipulation and analysis of the generation process.
papers.conclusion: The presented framework provides a method for interpreting audio generative models by mapping latent representations to acoustic properties via sparse autoencoders and linear probes, enabling both control and a better understanding of music generation.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features naturally align with acoustic properties in a near-linear fashion, enabling controllable audio manipulation via derived control vectors.
Linear probe accuracy reveals a hierarchy of decodability: pitch is most linearly separable, followed by loudness, while timbre remains challenging across models.
Analysis of the DiffRhythm generation process shows pitch converges first, followed by timbre, with loudness converging last, indicating a coarse-to-fine progression.
Different audio latent spaces (continuous VAE vs. discrete codecs) exhibit distinct sparsity characteristics and linear decodability for acoustic properties.
The framework successfully isolates targeted acoustic attribute edits while preserving non-targeted properties in generated audio.
future_direction: Apply the method to other generative architectures such as RAVE, ACE-Step, and AudioLDM.
Train probes for richer audio features including rhythm, harmony, and instrument identity.
Use the interpretable features to directly guide generation behavior during inference for fine-grained control.
papers.abstract: While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) successfully extract interpretable features from language models, applying them to audio generation faces unique challenges: audio's dense nature requires compression that obscures semantic meaning, and automatic feature characterization remains limited. We propose a framework for interpreting audio generative models by mapping their latent representations to human-interpretable acoustic concepts. We train SAEs on audio autoencoder latents, then learn linear mappings from SAE features to discretized acoustic properties (pitch, amplitude, and timbre). This enables both controllable manipulation and analysis of the AI music generation process, revealing how acoustic properties emerge during synthesis. We validate our approach on continuous (DiffRhythm-VAE) and discrete (EnCodec, WavTokenizer) audio latent spaces, and analyze DiffRhythm, a state-of-the-art text-to-music model, to demonstrate how pitch, timbre, and loudness evolve throughout generation. While our work is only done on audio modality, our framework can be extended to interpretable analysis of visual latent space generation models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Sequential Recommendation Models: Interpretation and Flexible Control
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret and control sequential recommendation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends sparse autoencoders to sequential recommendation models, providing methods for interpreting learned features and enabling flexible control over model predictions by steering feature activations.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are an effective tool for interpreting and controlling sequential recommendation models, learning interpretable features that align with item attributes and enabling flexible steering of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAE learns interpretable features that align with item attributes such as genres, and these features are more interpretable than the original transformer layer neurons.
SAE features are often monosemantic, correlating strongly with one or a few semantically related attributes.
Steering SAE feature activations allows for flexible control over model predictions, enabling increase or decrease of specific attributes in recommendations.
The control method works reliably across different datasets and models, and has a measurable impact on recommendation metrics.
SAE can capture diverse and meaningful patterns beyond predefined attributes, such as specific movie series or release years.
papers.abstract: Many current state-of-the-art models for sequential recommendations are based on transformer architectures. Interpretation and explanation of such black box models is an important research question, as a better understanding of their internals can help understand, influence, and control their behavior, which is very important in a variety of real-world applications. Recently, sparse autoencoders (SAE) have been shown to be a promising unsupervised approach to extract interpretable features from neural networks. In this work, we extend SAE to sequential recommender systems and propose a framework for interpreting and controlling model representations. We show that this approach can be successfully applied to the transformer trained on a sequential recommendation task: directions learned in such an unsupervised regime turn out to be more interpretable and monosemantic than the original hidden state dimensions. Further, we demonstrate a straightforward way to effectively and flexibly control the model's behavior, giving developers and users of recommendation systems the ability to adjust their recommendations to various custom scenarios and contexts.

papers.title: CE-Bench: Towards a Reliable Contrastive Evaluation Benchmark of Interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we create a reliable, LLM-free benchmark to evaluate the interpretability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CE-Bench, a fully LLM-free, contrastive evaluation benchmark for sparse autoencoders that measures interpretability via activation differences across curated story pairs, achieving strong alignment with existing LLM-assisted benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CE-Bench is a stable, deterministic, and reproducible framework for evaluating sparse autoencoder interpretability without relying on external LLMs, closely aligning with existing benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
CE-Bench achieves over 70% Spearman correlation with SAEBench rankings, providing a reliable LLM-free alternative.
Top-k and p-anneal SAE architectures consistently yield the highest interpretability scores.
Wider latent spaces (e.g., 65k dimensions) lead to higher interpretability scores, suggesting better feature disentanglement.
Interpretability scores are largely invariant to the type of transformer sub-layer (attention, MLP, residual) being probed.
Middle transformer layers (e.g., layers 10 and 15) provide the clearest semantic representations and highest interpretability scores.
papers.limitation:
The dataset of 5000 contrastive story pairs was generated using GPT-4, which may bias the evaluation toward models that capture GPT-4's stylistic and semantic regularities.
The dataset is limited in domain coverage, focusing mainly on synthetic narrative text, so its generalizability to varied or domain-specific contexts is uncertain.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach for uncovering interpretable features in large language models (LLMs). While several automated evaluation methods exist for SAEs, most rely on external LLMs. In this work, we introduce CE-Bench, a novel and lightweight contrastive evaluation benchmark for sparse autoencoders, built on a curated dataset of contrastive story pairs. We conduct comprehensive evaluation studies to validate the effectiveness of our approach. Our results show that CE-Bench reliably measures the interpretability of sparse autoencoders and aligns well with existing benchmarks without requiring an external LLM judge, achieving over 70% Spearman correlation with results in SAEBench. The official implementation and evaluation dataset are open-sourced and publicly available.

papers.title: SplInterp: Improving our Understanding and Training of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the theoretical understanding and training of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) using spline theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies spline theory to understand SAEs, showing they are piecewise affine splines that generalize k-means autoencoders, and introduces the PAM-SGD training algorithm which improves sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.conclusion: The spline theory lens provides insight into SAEs, and PAM-SGD is a promising training method with advantages in sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs are piecewise affine splines, and TopK SAEs correspond to Kth-order power diagrams.
SAEs generalize k-means autoencoders but sacrifice accuracy for interpretability compared to the optimal piecewise affine autoencoder (which combines k-means with local PCA).
The proposed PAM-SGD algorithm for training SAEs has solid theoretical foundations and shows promising empirical results, especially in low-data regimes and improved sparsity.
papers.limitation:
The spline geometry characterization is currently limited to TopK SAEs.
The bridge between SAEs and PCA-based autoencoders sets aside the matter of shared decoding vectors.
PAM-SGD makes approximations that break assumptions of the theory and had some empirical limitations (e.g., instability with TopK in LLM experiments).
future_direction: Extending the spline geometry characterization beyond TopK SAEs.
Exploring the incorporation of geometry into SAE training.
Studying the optimal autoencoding with shared decoding vectors and understanding more deeply the pros and cons of PAM-SGD.
