Our algorithm precisely predicts 26 out of 29 new sequences for the structures extracted from the Rfam dataset, while the other four algorithms predict no more than 22 out of 29. The proposed algorithm is comparable to the above algorithms on RNA-SSD datasets, where they can predict up to 33 appropriate sequences for RNA secondary structures out of 34.

papers.title: Uncovering the Folding Landscape of RNA Secondary Structure with Deep Graph Embeddings
papers.abstract: Biomolecular graph analysis has recently gained much attention in the emerging field of geometric deep learning. Here we focus on organizing biomolecular graphs in ways that expose meaningful relations and variations between them. We propose a geometric scattering autoencoder (GSAE) network for learning such graph embeddings. Our embedding network first extracts rich graph features using the recently proposed geometric scattering transform. Then, it leverages a semi-supervised variational autoencoder to extract a low-dimensional embedding that retains the information in these features that enable prediction of molecular properties as well as characterize graphs. We show that GSAE organizes RNA graphs both by structure and energy, accurately reflecting bistable RNA structures. Also, the model is generative and can sample new folding trajectories.

papers.title: On the importance of cotranscriptional RNA structure formation
papers.abstract: The expression of genes, both coding and noncoding, can be significantly influenced by RNA structural features of their corresponding transcripts. There is by now mounting experimental and some theoretical evidence that structure formation in vivo starts during transcription and that this cotranscriptional folding determines the functional RNA structural features that are being formed. Several decades of research in bioinformatics have resulted in a wide range of computational methods for predicting RNA secondary structures. Almost all state-of-the-art methods in terms of prediction accuracy, however, completely ignore the process of structure formation and focus exclusively on the final RNA structure. This review hopes to bridge this gap. We summarize the existing evidence for cotranscriptional folding and then review the different, currently used strategies for RNA secondary-structure prediction. Finally, we propose a range of ideas on how state-of-the-art methods could be potentially improved by explicitly capturing the process of cotranscriptional structure formation.

papers.title: RNA Pseudoknotted Structure Prediction Using Stochastic Multiple Context-Free Grammar
papers.abstract: Many attempts have so far been made at modeling RNA secondary structure by formal grammars. In a grammatical approach, secondary structure prediction can be viewed as parsing problem. However, there may be many different derivation trees for an input sequence. Thus, it is necessary to have a method of extracting biologically realistic derivation trees among them. One solution to this problem is to extend a grammar to a probabilistic model and find the most likely derivation tree, and another is to take free energy minimization into account. One simple formalism for describing RNA folding is context-free grammars(CFGs), but it is known that CFGs cannot represent pseudoknots. Therefore, several formal grammars have been proposed for modeling RNA pseudoknotted structure. In this paper, we focus on multiple context-free grammars (MCFGs), which are natural extension of CFGs and can represent pseudoknots, and extend MCFGs to a probabilistic model called stochastic MCFG (SMCFG). We present a polynomial time parsing algorithm for finding the most probable derivation tree, which is applicable to RNA secondary structure prediction including pseudoknots. Also, we propose a probability parameter estimation algorithm based on the EM (expectation maximization) algorithm. Finally, we show some experimental results on RNA pseudoknot prediction using the SMCFG parsing algorithm, which show good prediction accuracy.

papers.title: SentRNA: Improving computational RNA design by incorporating a prior of human design strategies
papers.abstract: Solving the RNA inverse folding problem is a critical prerequisite to RNA design, an emerging field in bioengineering with a broad range of applications from reaction catalysis to cancer therapy. Although significant progress has been made in developing machine-based inverse RNA folding algorithms, current approaches still have difficulty designing sequences for large or complex targets. On the other hand, human players of the online RNA design game EteRNA have consistently shown superior performance in this regard, being able to readily design sequences for targets that are challenging for machine algorithms. Here we present a novel approach to the RNA design problem, SentRNA, a design agent consisting of a fully-connected neural network trained end-to-end using human-designed RNA sequences. We show that through this approach, SentRNA can solve complex targets previously unsolvable by any machine-based approach and achieve state-of-the-art performance on two separate challenging test sets. Our results demonstrate that incorporating human design strategies into a design algorithm can significantly boost machine performance and suggests a new paradigm for machine-based RNA design.

papers.title: Ribonanza: deep learning of RNA structure through dual crowdsourcing
papers.abstract: Prediction of RNA structure from sequence remains an unsolved problem, and progress has been slowed by a paucity of experimental data. Here, we present Ribonanza, a dataset of chemical mapping measurements on two million diverse RNA sequences collected through Eterna and other crowdsourced initiatives. Ribonanza measurements enabled solicitation, training, and prospective evaluation of diverse deep neural networks through a Kaggle challenge, followed by distillation into a single, self-contained model called RibonanzaNet. When fine tuned on auxiliary datasets, RibonanzaNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in modeling experimental sequence dropout, RNA hydrolytic degradation, and RNA secondary structure, with implications for modeling RNA tertiary structure.

papers.title: Secondary-Structure-Informed RNA Inverse Design via Relational Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: RNA inverse design is an essential part of many RNA therapeutic strategies. To date, there have been great advances in computationally driven RNA design. The current machine learning approaches can predict the sequence of an RNA given its 3D structure with acceptable accuracy and at tremendous speed. The design and engineering of RNA regulators such as riboswitches, however, is often more difficult, partly due to their inherent conformational switching abilities. Although recent state-of-the-art models do incorporate information about the multiple structures that a sequence can fold into, there is great room for improvement in modeling structural switching. In this work, a relational geometric graph neural network is proposed that explicitly incorporates alternative structures to predict an RNA sequence. Converting the RNA structure into a geometric graph, the proposed model uses edge types to distinguish between the primary structure, secondary structure, and spatial positioning of the nucleotides in representing structures. The results show higher native sequence recovery rates over those of gRNAde across different test sets (eg. 72% vs. 66%) and a benchmark from the literature (60% vs. 57%). Secondary-structure edge types had a more significant impact on the sequence recovery than the spatial edge types as defined in this work. Overall, these results suggest the need for more complex and case-specific characterization of RNA for successful inverse design.

papers.title: Novel representation of RNA secondary structure used to improve prediction algorithms
papers.abstract: We propose a novel representation of RNA secondary structure for a quick comparison of different structures. Secondary structure was viewed as a set of stems and each stem was represented by two values according to its position. Using this representation, we improved the comparative sequence analysis method results and the minimum free-energy model. In the comparative sequence analysis method, a novel algorithm independent of multiple sequence alignment was developed to improve performance. When dealing with a single-RNA sequence, the minimum free-energy model is improved by combining it with RNA class information. Secondary structure prediction experiments were done on tRNA and RNAse P RNA; sensitivity and specificity were both improved. Furthermore, software programs were developed for non-commercial use.

papers.title: Predicting RNA secondary structure via adaptive deep recurrent neural networks with energy-based filter
papers.abstract: Comparative experiments conducted on an authoritative dataset RNA STRAND (RNA secondary STRucture and statistical Analysis Database) revealed a 12% higher accuracy relative to three currently used methods.

papers.title: RNA SECONDARY STRUCTURE PREDICTION, A CUCKOO SEARCH APPROACH
papers.abstract: RNA secondary structure prediction uses techniques like crystallography, NMR spectroscopy etc. Computation based techniques estimate the possible base pairs that could be formed in RNA. Soft computing techniques generally select some random pair or pair sequences and then check them according to some parameters. The final sequence of RNA which is closest to the required fitness is selected as the final structure. The cuckoo search approach is good for finding the feasible search space locations. Cuckoo search approach feasibly provides results for the detection of base pairs in the RNA and the RNA secondary structure.

papers.title: LinearFold: Linear-Time Prediction of RNA Secondary Structures
papers.abstract: Predicting the secondary structure of an RNA sequence with speed and accuracy is useful in many applications such as drug design. The state-of-the-art predictors have a fundamental limitation: they have a run time that scales cubically with the length of the input sequence, which is slow for longer RNAs and limits the use of secondary structure prediction in genome-wide applications. To address this bottleneck, we designed the first linear-time algorithm for this problem. which can be used with both thermodynamic and machine-learned scoring functions. Our algorithm, like previous work, is based on dynamic programming (DP), but with two crucial differences: (a) we incrementally process the sequence in a left-to-right rather than in a bottom-up fashion, and (b) because of this incremental processing, we can further employ beam search pruning to ensure linear run time in practice (with the cost of exact search). Even though our search is approximate, surprisingly, it results in even higher overall accuracy on a diverse database of sequences with known structures. More interestingly, it leads to significantly more accurate predictions on the longest sequence families in that database (16S and 23S Ribosomal RNAs), as well as improved accuracies for long-range base pairs (500+ nucleotides apart).

papers.title: RNA-Puzzles : A CASP-like evaluation of RNA three-dimensional structure prediction
papers.abstract: We report the results of a first, collective, blind experiment in RNA three-dimensional (3D) structure prediction, encompassing three prediction puzzles. The goals are to assess the leading edge of RNA structure prediction techniques; compare existing methods and tools; and evaluate their relative strengths, weaknesses, and limitations in terms of sequence length and structural complexity. The results should give potential users insight into the suitability of available methods for different applications and facilitate efforts in the RNA structure prediction community in ongoing efforts to improve prediction tools. We also report the creation of an automated evaluation pipeline to facilitate the analysis of future RNA structure prediction exercises.

papers.title: Superposition of target structures enables design of bi-stable RNA molecules with deep learning
papers.abstract: Abstract The ability to design RNA molecules with specific structures and functions could facilitate research and developments in biotechnology, biology and pharmacy. Here we present a flexible RNA design framework based on deep learning that locally optimizes sequences by gradient-guided search methods. We demonstrate its effectiveness by designing bi-stable RNA molecules by superimposing conformer target structures.

papers.title: Accurate prediction of RNA secondary structure including pseudoknots through solving minimum-cost flow with learned potentials
papers.abstract: Pseudoknots are key structure motifs of RNA and pseudoknotted RNAs play important roles in a variety of biological processes. Here, we present KnotFold, an accurate approach to the prediction of RNA secondary structure including pseudoknots. The key elements of KnotFold include a learned potential function and a minimum-cost flow algorithm to find the secondary structure with the lowest potential. KnotFold learns the potential from the RNAs with known structures using an attention-based neural network, thus avoiding the inaccuracy of hand-crafted energy functions. The specially designed minimum-cost flow algorithm used by KnotFold considers all possible combinations of base pairs and selects from them the optimal combination. The algorithm breaks the restriction of nested base pairs required by the widely used dynamic programming algorithms, thus enabling the identification of pseudoknots. Using 1,009 pseudoknotted RNAs as representatives, we demonstrate the successful application of KnotFold in predicting RNA secondary structures including pseudoknots with accuracy higher than the state-of-the-art approaches. We anticipate that KnotFold, with its superior accuracy, will greatly facilitate the understanding of RNA structures and functionalities.

papers.title: A Comparative Taxonomy of Parallel Algorithms for RNA Secondary Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: RNA molecules have been discovered playing crucial roles in numerous biological and medical procedures and processes. RNA structures determination have become a major problem in the biology context. Recently, computer scientists have empowered the biologists with RNA secondary structures that ease an understanding of the RNA functions and roles. Detecting RNA secondary structure is an NP-hard problem, especially in pseudoknotted RNA structures. The detection process is also time-consuming; as a result, an alternative approach such as using parallel architectures is a desirable option. The main goal in this paper is to do an intensive investigation of parallel methods used in the literature to solve the demanding issues, related to the RNA secondary structure prediction methods. Then, we introduce a new taxonomy for the parallel RNA folding methods. Based on this proposed taxonomy, a systematic and scientific comparison is performed among these existing methods.

papers.title: RNA secondary structure packages evaluated and improved by high-throughput experiments
papers.abstract: Abstract The computer-aided study and design of RNA molecules is increasingly prevalent across a range of disciplines, yet little is known about the accuracy of commonly used structure modeling packages in tasks sensitive to ensemble properties of RNA. Here, we demonstrate that the EternaBench dataset, a set of over 20,000 synthetic RNA constructs designed in iterative cycles on the RNA design platform Eterna, provides incisive discriminative power in evaluating current packages in ensemble-oriented structure prediction tasks. We find that CONTRAfold and RNAsoft, packages with parameters derived through statistical learning, achieve consistently higher accuracy than more widely used packages in their standard settings, which derive parameters primarily from thermodynamic experiments. Motivated by these results, we develop a multitask-learning-based model, EternaFold, which demonstrates improved performance that generalizes to diverse external datasets, including complete mRNAs and viral genomes probed in human cells and synthetic designs modeling mRNA vaccines.

papers.title: Uncovering the Folding Landscape of RNA Secondary Structure with Deep\n Graph Embeddings
papers.abstract:
Biomolecular graph analysis has recently gained much attention in the
emerging field of geometric deep learning. Here we focus on organizing
biomolecular graphs in ways that expose meaningful relations and variations
between them. We propose a geometric scattering autoencoder (GSAE) network for
learning such graph embeddings. Our embedding network first extracts rich graph
features using the recently proposed geometric scattering transform. Then, it
leverages a semi-supervised variational autoencoder to extract a
low-dimensional embedding that retains the information in these features that
enable prediction of molecular properties as well as characterize graphs. We
show that GSAE organizes RNA graphs both by structure and energy, accurately
reflecting bistable RNA structures. Also, the model is generative and can
sample new folding trajectories.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret the internal representations of protein language models and steer them to generate sequences with desired features?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can be applied to protein language models to interpret their internal representations and that the identified latent features can be used to steer the model to generate protein sequences with desired structural motifs.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising approach for interpreting and controlling protein language models, opening new avenues for protein design and engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders trained on ESM-2 activations can identify latent components associated with protein annotations such as transmembrane regions, binding sites, and zinc finger motifs.
A heuristic based on intrinsic dimension estimation can guide the selection of the transformer layer from which to extract representations for SAE training.
Intervening on specific latent components during inference can steer the model to generate protein sequences that contain desired features, such as zinc finger domains.
The sequence generation pipeline successfully produced sequences with zinc finger motifs, though it requires parameter tuning to improve success rates.
papers.limitation:
The sequence generation pipeline requires parameter fine-tuning to improve the success rate.
The features learned by the model may not directly align with manually curated dataset annotations, as latents might encode more specific or coarse-grained features.
future_direction: Extend these methods to larger models and a wider range of protein features.
Automate the parameter search for the sequence generation pipeline to improve efficiency.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancements in transformer-based language models have revolutionized natural language processing, yet understanding the internal mechanisms of these models remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the application of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to interpret the internal representations of protein language models, specifically focusing on the ESM-2 8M parameter model. By performing a statistical analysis on each latent component's relevance to distinct protein annotations, we identify potential interpretations linked to various protein characteristics, including transmembrane regions, binding sites, and specialized motifs. We then leverage these insights to guide sequence generation, shortlisting the relevant latent components that can steer the model towards desired targets such as zinc finger domains. This work contributes to the emerging field of mechanistic interpretability in biological sequence models, offering new perspectives on model steering for sequence design.

papers.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What do protein language models (PLMs) learn internally, and how can we extract and analyze interpretable features from their representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic framework using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract and analyze interpretable features from protein language models, revealing features that correlate with known biological concepts and enabling applications like filling missing annotations and steering sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Protein language models encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology, and the SAE-based framework successfully extracts these features, recovering both known biology and potentially new protein motifs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture significantly more biological annotations (up to 2,548 features per layer) than individual neurons in ESM-2 (up to 46 per layer).
Features cluster based on shared functional and structural roles, revealing hierarchical relationships and subtle specializations.
Large language models (Claude-3.5 Sonnet) can generate meaningful descriptions of SAE features, with high correlation between predicted and actual activation patterns.
Feature activation patterns can identify missing annotations in protein databases and suggest novel biological motifs.
Targeted steering of specific feature activations can influence the model's sequence predictions in interpretable ways.
papers.limitation:
Scaling this approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold is a crucial next step.
Steering experiments are currently limited to simple contexts (e.g., periodic glycine patterns); extending steering to more complex biological concepts remains challenging.
The analysis focuses only on representations of unmasked amino acids, leaving open questions about masked token embeddings and the CLS token.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold.
Improving feature interpretability through advances in SAE training and additional evaluation metrics.
Mapping how features combine into interpretable circuits for specific capabilities like 3D contact prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify up to 2,548 human-interpretable latent features per layer that strongly correlate with up to 143 known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals up to 46 neurons per layer with clear conceptual alignment across 15 known concepts, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to extract and analyze these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for exploring and analyzing learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: SAE-RNA: A Sparse Autoencoder Model for Interpreting RNA Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How and what do RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-RNA, a sparse autoencoder model that interprets RNA language model representations by discovering sparse features aligned with biological structures and ncRNA families.
papers.conclusion: SAE-RNA provides a method for concept discovery in pretrained RNA LM embeddings, enabling interpretation without retraining and offering features for downstream tasks like feature-aware fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features localize in structurally meaningful regions such as stems and hairpins.
Features exhibit sequence biases like poly-G/C/A/U tracts that map onto secondary-structure contexts.
Deeper layers transition from diffuse to type-selective activations, with a small subset of channels preferentially firing for specific ncRNA families.
The last layer shows diminished signal, suggesting late-stage representational compression.
Features can be annotated using LLM prompting to align with known biological motifs.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints restricted the scale of training data used for the SAE models.
SAE training outcomes can vary depending on hyperparameter choices, such as sparsity setting, which may influence the granularity and stability of learned features.
future_direction: Feature-aware fine-tuning with SAE-derived features for downstream RNA tasks.
papers.abstract: Deep learning, particularly with the advancement of Large Language Models, has transformed biomolecular modeling, with protein advances (e.g., ESM) inspiring emerging RNA language models such as RiNALMo. Yet how and what these RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families remains unclear. We present SAE- RNA, interpretability model that analyzes RiNALMo representations and maps them to known human-level biological features. Our work frames RNA interpretability as concept discovery in pretrained embeddings, without end-to-end retraining, and provides practical tools to probe what RNA LMs may encode about ncRNA families. The model can be extended to close comparisons between RNA groups, and supporting hypothesis generation about previously unrecognized relationships.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why directly applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two main reasons why sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide misleading decompositions of steering vectors: (1) steering vectors are out-of-distribution for SAEs, and (2) SAEs cannot represent negative coefficients which are meaningful in steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading due to out-of-distribution and non-negativity constraints; alternative approaches such as learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors have significantly smaller L2-norms than model activations, causing the SAE encoder bias to dominate the decomposition and yield misleading results.
Scaling steering vectors does not resolve the out-of-distribution issue because steering vectors lack default components present in model activations.
SAEs restrict decompositions to non-negative coefficients, but steering vectors have meaningful negative projections in feature directions.
Negative projections in steering vectors can cause spurious positive activations in SAE features due to negative cosine similarities between features.
These issues explain prior observations of irrelevant features in SAE decompositions and the failure of SAE-reconstructed vectors to retain steering properties.
papers.limitation:
The proposed alternative method of learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis requires two SAE decompositions per difference vector, increasing the potential impact of SAE error.
The corrigibility steering vectors may include confounding features related to computer science and language modeling.
future_direction: Explore learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis and establish evaluation metrics to compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to control the behaviour of large language models. However, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may offer a potential method to interpret steering vectors, recent findings show that SAE-reconstructed vectors often lack the steering properties of the original vectors. This paper investigates why directly applying SAEs to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions, identifying two reasons: (1) steering vectors fall outside the input distribution for which SAEs are designed, and (2) steering vectors can have meaningful negative projections in feature directions, which SAEs are not designed to accommodate. These limitations hinder the direct use of SAEs for interpreting steering vectors.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable Structure in Small Gene Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models, revealing features like nucleotide identity and transcription factor binding motifs, demonstrating that compact models learn structured genomic representations.
papers.conclusion: SAEs can extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models, highlighting their ability to capture essential genomic features.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs extracted sparse features corresponding to individual nucleotides with high precision.
SAEs identified features aligned with known transcription factor binding motifs, such as MA1596.1 and MA0052.5.
Even compact models effectively capture transcription factor binding specificity.
The recall variability indicates the complexity and redundancy of regulatory elements in genomic sequences.
future_direction: Extend SAE approach to other genomic contexts like non-coding regions or species-specific variations.
Explore SAEs for model refinement and interpretability across different architectures.
Apply SAEs to other biological modalities like single-cell gene expression and multi-omics datasets.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs), revealing latent latent features with semantical meaning. This interpretability has also proven valuable in biological domains: applying SAEs to protein language models uncovered meaningful features related to protein structure and function. More recently, SAEs have been used to analyze genomics-focused models such as Evo 2, identifying interpretable features in gene sequences. However, it remains unclear whether SAEs can extract meaningful representations from small gene language models, which have fewer parameters and potentially less expressive capacity. To address it, we propose applying SAEs to the activations of a small gene language model. We demonstrate that even small-scale models encode biologically relevant genomic features, such as transcription factor binding motifs, that SAEs can effectively uncover. Our findings suggest that compact gene language models are capable of learning structured genomic representations, and that SAEs offer a scalable approach for interpreting gene models across various model sizes.

papers.title: ProtSAE: Disentangling and Interpreting Protein Language Models via Semantically-Guided Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle semantic features in protein language models to improve interpretability and enable precise model control?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ProtSAE, a semantically-guided sparse autoencoder that disentangles protein features and aligns them with biological concepts, improving interpretability and enabling steering of protein language models.
papers.conclusion: ProtSAE effectively disentangles semantic features in protein language models, leading to better interpretability and control for protein engineering tasks.
papers.key_findings:
ProtSAE learns more biologically relevant and interpretable hidden features compared to previous SAE methods.
ProtSAE maintains high reconstruction fidelity while achieving better results in interpretable probing.
ProtSAE enables effective steering of PLM outputs for downstream generation tasks.
Ablation studies show that the semantic guidance components (annotation data and domain knowledge) are crucial for performance.
papers.limitation: ProtSAE is only evaluated on ESM2 and not scaled to broader architectures or application scenarios.
future_direction: Extend ProtSAE to protein language models aligned with natural language.
Apply ProtSAE to sequence-structure co-design models.
Explore interpretable feature extraction from protein structure prediction models and generative diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) has emerged as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability of large language models. Recent works apply SAE to protein language models (PLMs), aiming to extract and analyze biologically meaningful features from their latent spaces. However, SAE suffers from semantic entanglement, where individual neurons often mix multiple nonlinear concepts, making it difficult to reliably interpret or manipulate model behaviors. In this paper, we propose a semantically-guided SAE, called ProtSAE. Unlike existing SAE which requires annotation datasets to filter and interpret activations, we guide semantic disentanglement during training using both annotation datasets and domain knowledge to mitigate the effects of entangled attributes. We design interpretability experiments showing that ProtSAE learns more biologically relevant and interpretable hidden features compared to previous methods. Performance analyses further demonstrate that ProtSAE maintains high reconstruction fidelity while achieving better results in interpretable probing. We also show the potential of ProtSAE in steering PLMs for downstream generation tasks.

papers.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders to large language models and how should we evaluate their quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for scaling sparse autoencoders using a TopK activation function to directly control sparsity and techniques to prevent dead latents, establishes scaling laws, and proposes new metrics for evaluating feature quality.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can be scaled effectively with the proposed methods, and larger autoencoders yield better features according to the introduced evaluation metrics.
papers.key_findings:
TopK activation function improves the reconstruction-sparsity frontier and simplifies training compared to ReLU autoencoders with L1 penalty.
Techniques like tied initialization and an auxiliary loss reduce dead latents to 7% in a 16 million latent autoencoder.
Clean scaling laws are found with respect to autoencoder size and sparsity.
Larger autoencoders generally improve feature quality according to new metrics (probe loss, explainability, ablation sparsity).
The method scales to training a 16 million latent autoencoder on GPT-4 activations.
papers.limitation:
The probe-based evaluation metric leans on strong assumptions about what kinds of features are natural.
Evaluating explanation precision for arbitrary English explanations is computationally expensive.
future_direction: Explore ways to make it more tractable to approximate precision for arbitrary English explanations.
Scale to even larger autoencoders and apply the method to other models and modalities.
Improve evaluation metrics for feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising unsupervised approach for extracting interpretable features from a language model by reconstructing activations from a sparse bottleneck layer. Since language models learn many concepts, autoencoders need to be very large to recover all relevant features. However, studying the properties of autoencoder scaling is difficult due to the need to balance reconstruction and sparsity objectives and the presence of dead latents. We propose using k-sparse autoencoders [Makhzani and Frey, 2013] to directly control sparsity, simplifying tuning and improving the reconstruction-sparsity frontier. Additionally, we find modifications that result in few dead latents, even at the largest scales we tried. Using these techniques, we find clean scaling laws with respect to autoencoder size and sparsity. We also introduce several new metrics for evaluating feature quality based on the recovery of hypothesized features, the explainability of activation patterns, and the sparsity of downstream effects. These metrics all generally improve with autoencoder size. To demonstrate the scalability of our approach, we train a 16 million latent autoencoder on GPT-4 activations for 40 billion tokens. We release training code and autoencoders for open-source models, as well as a visualizer.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: Temporal Sparse Autoencoders: Leveraging the Sequential Nature of Language for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate temporal consistency into sparse autoencoders to better recover high-level semantic features in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs) that incorporate a temporal contrastive loss to encourage consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens, leading to better disentanglement of semantic and syntactic features in language models.
papers.conclusion: Temporal SAEs leverage the sequential nature of language to better extract semantic features, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.
papers.key_findings:
T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
T-SAEs exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal.
T-SAEs show improved disentanglement between high-level (semantic) and low-level (syntactic) features.
T-SAEs provide practical interpretability benefits, such as in safety monitoring and steering.
papers.abstract: Translating the internal representations and computations of models into concepts that humans can understand is a key goal of interpretability. While recent dictionary learning methods such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising route to discover human-interpretable features, they suffer from a variety of problems, including a systematic failure to capture the rich conceptual information that drives linguistic understanding. Instead, they exhibit a bias towards shallow, token-specific, or noisy features, such as "the phrase 'The' at the start of sentences". In this work, we propose that this is due to a fundamental issue with how dictionary learning methods for LLMs are trained. Language itself has a rich, well-studied structure spanning syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; however, current unsupervised methods largely ignore this linguistic knowledge, leading to poor feature discovery that favors superficial patterns over meaningful concepts. We focus on a simple but important aspect of language: semantic content has long-range dependencies and tends to be smooth over a sequence, whereas syntactic information is much more local. Building on this insight, we introduce Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs), which incorporate a novel contrastive loss encouraging consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens. This simple yet powerful modification enables SAEs to disentangle semantic from syntactic features in a self-supervised manner. Across multiple datasets and models, T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Strikingly, they exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: PolySAE: Modeling Feature Interactions in Sparse Autoencoders via Polynomial Decoding
papers.research_question: How can we extend sparse autoencoders to model non-linear feature interactions (compositional structure) while preserving a linear encoder for interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PolySAE, a sparse autoencoder that extends the decoder with quadratic and cubic terms to model feature interactions via low-rank tensor factorization, improving feature separation and probing performance while maintaining reconstruction fidelity.
papers.conclusion: PolySAE effectively models feature interactions in sparse autoencoders, capturing compositional structure beyond linear combinations and improving interpretability without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
papers.key_findings:
PolySAE achieves an average improvement of approximately 8% in probing F1 across four language models and three SAE variants while maintaining comparable reconstruction error.
PolySAE produces 2–10× larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions, indicating more separated semantic structure.
Learned interaction weights exhibit negligible correlation with co-occurrence frequency (r=0.06), suggesting they capture compositional structure rather than surface statistics.
PolySAE adds a small parameter overhead (3% for GPT-2 small) through low-rank factorization of interaction terms.
Qualitative analysis shows PolySAE captures compositional structures like morphological binding (e.g., 'administrators') and phrasal composition (e.g., 'Starbucks').
papers.limitation: The study is limited to models up to 2B parameters and experiments are restricted to forced-sparsity SAE variants.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method for interpreting neural network representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of dictionary atoms. However, SAEs assume that features combine additively through linear reconstruction, an assumption that cannot capture compositional structure: linear models cannot distinguish whether "Starbucks" arises from the composition of "star" and "coffee" features or merely their co-occurrence. This forces SAEs to allocate monolithic features for compound concepts rather than decomposing them into interpretable constituents. We introduce PolySAE, which extends the SAE decoder with higher-order terms to model feature interactions while preserving the linear encoder essential for interpretability. Through low-rank tensor factorization on a shared projection subspace, PolySAE captures pairwise and triple feature interactions with small parameter overhead (3% on GPT2). Across four language models and three SAE variants, PolySAE achieves an average improvement of approximately 8% in probing F1 while maintaining comparable reconstruction error, and produces 2-10$\times$ larger Wasserstein distances between class-conditional feature distributions. Critically, learned interaction weights exhibit negligible correlation with co-occurrence frequency ($r = 0.06$ vs. $r = 0.82$ for SAE feature covariance), suggesting that polynomial terms capture compositional structure, such as morphological binding and phrasal composition, largely independent of surface statistics.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders make sense of gene expression latent variable models?
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be effectively used to interpret latent representations in biological data, specifically single-cell gene expression data?
papers.core_contribution: This work explores the potential of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting latent representations in biological data, introduces scFeatureLens for automated annotation of SAE features with biological concepts, and demonstrates that SAEs can extract meaningful features that steer cells into desired biological programs.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that SAEs are a valuable tool for interpreting latent representations in biological data, and the introduced scFeatureLens pipeline provides a scalable framework for improved interpretability in single-cell analysis, though more research is needed in this field.
papers.key_findings:
Distribution type and distance of hidden generative variables affect their recovery from latent representations.
SAEs can extract meaningful features from single-cell expression models that successfully steer cells into desired programs, with features acting either locally or globally.
SAEs can uncover subtle biological signals that might otherwise be missed in traditional analysis.
The introduced automated pipeline, scFeatureLens, enables large-scale interpretability analysis by linking SAE features to biological concepts from gene sets.
SAEs do not provide an advantage over simple baselines for recovering known features, but are valuable for discovering unknown features and data generation structure.
papers.limitation:
Variables with an indirect effect on the observed data and little structure in the generative process could practically not be recovered.
SAEs do not pose an advantage in the recovery of known or hypothesized features compared to simple baselines.
The case study was limited to Gene Ontology terms which are incomplete and biased towards well-studied genes.
future_direction: Future work could explore metrics for evaluating the biological meaningfulness in and differences between embeddings.
More research is needed in the field of interpretability for biological models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have lately been used to uncover interpretable latent features in large language models. By projecting dense embeddings into a much higher-dimensional and sparse space, learned features become disentangled and easier to interpret. This work explores the potential of SAEs for decomposing embeddings in complex and high-dimensional biological data. Using simulated data, it outlines the efficacy, hyperparameter landscape, and limitations of SAEs when it comes to extracting ground truth generative variables from latent space. The application to embeddings from pretrained single-cell models shows that SAEs can find and steer key biological processes and even uncover subtle biological signals that might otherwise be missed. This work further introduces scFeatureLens, an automated interpretability approach for linking SAE features and biological concepts from gene sets to enable large-scale analysis and hypothesis generation in single-cell gene expression models.

papers.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders extract relatively monosemantic features that are more interpretable than neurons, with most features being human-understandable.
Features can be used to intervene on and steer transformer generation, such as activating specific features to produce corresponding text like base64 or Arabic script.
Features are universal across different models and autoencoder runs, more similar to each other than to neurons, suggesting they reflect underlying data properties.
Features split into families as autoencoder size increases, providing different resolutions of understanding the same model components.
Despite having only 512 neurons, the MLP layer can represent tens of thousands of features through superposition, as shown by scaling the autoencoder.
papers.abstract: How can language models be decomposed into interpretable, monosemantic features using dictionary learning to address polysemanticity and superposition? Sparse autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from language model activations, enabling decomposition into understandable components and facilitating circuit analysis. Dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders is a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, successfully decomposing language models into monosemantic features and revealing internal structures like feature clusters and automata-like systems.

papers.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable monosemantic features from polysemantic activations in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes PS-Eval, a new evaluation metric and dataset for assessing whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations. It finds that SAEs optimized for MSE-L0 Pareto frontier do not necessarily improve monosemantic feature extraction, and that deeper layers and attention mechanisms contribute to distinguishing polysemous words.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes Poly-Semantic Evaluation (PS-Eval), a new metric and dataset to assess the ability of SAEs to extract monosemantic features from polysemantic activations, in complement to traditional MSE or L0 metrics. The work encourages the community to conduct holistic evaluations of SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability and do not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features.
Deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word.
Increasing the latent dimension of SAEs generally improves specificity up to a saturation point.
Activation functions like TopK and JumpReLU, designed to improve MSE-L0 trade-off, do not perform well on PS-Eval metrics; ReLU performs best.
SAE features are more interpretable than raw LLM activations for polysemous words.
papers.limitation: PS-Eval relies on evaluating the maximum activation of SAE features, which may not always align with intended word meanings and could introduce ambiguity.
future_direction: Incorporate similarity metrics that utilize the distribution of SAE features, rather than relying solely on maximum activation.
Extend PS-Eval beyond natural language to other domains such as diffusion models and vision-language models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have gained a lot of attention as a promising tool to improve the interpretability of large language models (LLMs) by mapping the complex superposition of polysemantic neurons into monosemantic features and composing a sparse dictionary of words. However, traditional performance metrics like Mean Squared Error and L0 sparsity ignore the evaluation of the semantic representational power of SAEs -- whether they can acquire interpretable monosemantic features while preserving the semantic relationship of words. For instance, it is not obvious whether a learned sparse feature could distinguish different meanings in one word. In this paper, we propose a suite of evaluations for SAEs to analyze the quality of monosemantic features by focusing on polysemous words. Our findings reveal that SAEs developed to improve the MSE-L0 Pareto frontier may confuse interpretability, which does not necessarily enhance the extraction of monosemantic features. The analysis of SAEs with polysemous words can also figure out the internal mechanism of LLMs; deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word. Our semantics focused evaluation offers new insights into the polysemy and the existing SAE objective and contributes to the development of more practical SAEs.

papers.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the amortisation gap in sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and can more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that sparse autoencoder (SAE) encoders are inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference due to an amortisation gap, and demonstrates empirically that more expressive encoders (like MLPs) and sparse coding methods can outperform SAEs, leading to more interpretable features in large language models.
papers.conclusion: More sophisticated sparse inference methods, such as MLPs and sparse coding, can outperform traditional SAE encoders, reducing the amortisation gap and improving interpretability, which opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAE encoders have a provable amortisation gap, making them suboptimal for sparse inference even in solvable cases.
Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and sparse coding consistently outperform SAEs in recovering sparse codes, with sparse coding achieving the highest performance.
The performance advantage of more sophisticated methods is more pronounced in regimes where compressed sensing theory predicts recoverability.
These findings generalize to real-world applications, as shown by training on GPT-2 activations where MLPs yield more interpretable features than SAEs.
The amortisation gap can be reduced with increased compute, with MLPs surpassing SAE performance after a consistent computational threshold.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result on SAE suboptimality is proven for a specific setting (linear-nonlinear encoder, sparse signals in union of subspaces) and may not cover all practical SAE implementations.
future_direction: Pitting optimised sparse coding approaches (e.g., Least Angle Regression, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) against optimised SAE architectures.
Further exploration of top-k sparse coding with proper hyperparameter tuning to achieve Pareto improvements.
Scaling the methods to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work has shown promise in using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable features in neural network representations. However, the simple linear-nonlinear encoding mechanism in SAEs limits their ability to perform accurate sparse inference. Using compressed sensing theory, we prove that an SAE encoder is inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference, even in solvable cases. We then decouple encoding and decoding processes to empirically explore conditions where more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders. Our results reveal substantial performance gains with minimal compute increases in correct inference of sparse codes. We demonstrate this generalises to SAEs applied to large language models, where more expressive encoders achieve greater interpretability. This work opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations and analysing large language model activations.

papers.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to reduce biases like shrinkage and achieve better sparsity and reconstruction fidelity in language model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gated SAEs that decouple feature detection and magnitude estimation, solving shrinkage and providing Pareto improvements in sparsity and reconstruction fidelity over baseline SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Gated SAEs are a promising improvement for sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability, offering better performance and reduced biases.
papers.key_findings:
Gated SAEs achieve better reconstruction fidelity at any given level of sparsity compared to baseline SAEs.
Gated SAEs effectively address the shrinkage problem, with reconstructions being unbiased.
Gated SAE features are similarly interpretable to baseline SAE features based on human evaluation.
Ablation studies show that freezing the decoder in the auxiliary task and weight tying are important for performance.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are an effective technique for unsupervised discovery of interpretable features in language models' (LMs) activations, by finding sparse, linear reconstructions of LM activations. We introduce the Gated Sparse Autoencoder (Gated SAE), which achieves a Pareto improvement over training with prevailing methods. In SAEs, the L1 penalty used to encourage sparsity introduces many undesirable biases, such as shrinkage -- systematic underestimation of feature activations. The key insight of Gated SAEs is to separate the functionality of (a) determining which directions to use and (b) estimating the magnitudes of those directions: this enables us to apply the L1 penalty only to the former, limiting the scope of undesirable side effects. Through training SAEs on LMs of up to 7B parameters we find that, in typical hyper-parameter ranges, Gated SAEs solve shrinkage, are similarly interpretable, and require half as many firing features to achieve comparable reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: Unveiling Language-Specific Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to identify and analyze language-specific features in multilingual Large Language Models, and what is the impact of these features on model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify language-specific features in LLMs and demonstrates that these features can be used to enhance steering vectors for better control over the language generated by the models.
papers.conclusion: The study uses SAEs to analyze multilingual capabilities in LLMs, identifying language-specific features that play a crucial role in language generation and can be leveraged to enhance steering vectors for improved language control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can exhibit strong monolingual characteristics, as measured by a novel monolinguality metric.
Language-specific features are not only tied to language-specific tokens but also to the language-specific linguistic context, as shown in code-switching experiments.
Ablating language-specific features via directional ablation significantly reduces model performance only in the target language, leaving other languages largely unaffected.
Some languages have multiple synergistic features; ablating them together yields a greater performance impact than ablating them individually.
Using language-specific features as gating signals to improve steering vectors achieves better control over the language generated by LLMs, with improved performance and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The method does not yet cover certain low-resource languages.
The SAE-based steering vectors sometimes underperform compared to the original steering vectors.
The SAEs used were not trained on curated multilingual data.
future_direction: Utilize language-specific features to guide the training process of multilingual language models.
Investigate low-resource languages to enhance the analysis.
Explore more refined approaches to improve the performance of SAE-based steering vectors.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms behind multilingual capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) have been examined using neuron-based or internal-activation-based methods. However, these methods often face challenges such as superposition and layer-wise activation variance, which limit their reliability. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offer a more nuanced analysis by decomposing the activations of LLMs into a sparse linear combination of SAE features. We introduce a novel metric to assess the monolinguality of features obtained from SAEs, discovering that some features are strongly related to specific languages. Additionally, we show that ablating these SAE features only significantly reduces abilities in one language of LLMs, leaving others almost unaffected. Interestingly, we find some languages have multiple synergistic SAE features, and ablating them together yields greater improvement than ablating individually. Moreover, we leverage these SAE-derived language-specific features to enhance steering vectors, achieving control over the language generated by LLMs. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aatrox103/multilingual-llm-features.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering LLMs with Mutual Information-based Explanations on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to better explain sparse autoencoder features in LLMs to capture semantic meaning and use these explanations to steer LLM behaviors, particularly for defending against jailbreak attacks.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mutual information-based explanation method for sparse autoencoder features that mitigates frequency bias and enables effective steering of LLM behaviors, particularly for enhancing safety against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that discourse-level explanations from sparse autoencoders are crucial for understanding and steering LLM behaviors, particularly for safety applications.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical analysis reveals frequency bias in sparse autoencoder features between discourse topics and linguistic patterns.
The proposed mutual information-based method generates more discourse-level explanations compared to baseline methods like TopAct and N2G.
The discourse-level explanations are effective in steering LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks.
Experiments show a higher successful explained rate for features with the proposed method.
Steering strategies such as amplification and calibration can enhance LLM safety without additional model training.
papers.limitation: The approach relies on existing sparse autoencoders without modifying their architectures or training to mitigate frequency bias.
future_direction: Designing improved architectures or training objectives for sparse autoencoders to inherently mitigate frequency bias.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at handling human queries, but they can occasionally generate flawed or unexpected responses. Understanding their internal states is crucial for understanding their successes, diagnosing their failures, and refining their capabilities. Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise for interpreting LLM internal representations, limited research has explored how to better explain SAE features, i.e., understanding the semantic meaning of features learned by SAE. Our theoretical analysis reveals that existing explanation methods suffer from the frequency bias issue, where they emphasize linguistic patterns over semantic concepts, while the latter is more critical to steer LLM behaviors. To address this, we propose using a fixed vocabulary set for feature interpretations and designing a mutual information-based objective, aiming to better capture the semantic meaning behind these features. We further propose two runtime steering strategies that adjust the learned feature activations based on their corresponding explanations. Empirical results show that, compared to baselines, our method provides more discourse-level explanations and effectively steers LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks. These findings highlight the value of explanations for steering LLM behaviors in downstream applications. We will release our code and data once accepted.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be applied to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to improve interpretability and steerability, and how can we quantitatively evaluate the monosemanticity of neurons in such models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the MonoSemanticity score (MS) to evaluate neuron-level monosemanticity in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), validates MS with a human study, and demonstrates that SAEs can steer multimodal LLM outputs by intervening on vision encoder neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) effectively improve neuron-level monosemanticity in Vision-Language Models, with the MonoSemanticity score providing a reliable metric aligned with human judgment, and shows that SAEs enable unsupervised concept-based steering of multimodal LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs significantly increase the monosemanticity of individual neurons in VLMs compared to original neurons.
Sparsity and wider latent dimensions are the most influential factors for improving monosemanticity.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve overall superior monosemanticity scores compared to standard SAE variants.
SAE interventions on the vision encoder can steer multimodal LLM (e.g., LLaVA) outputs to insert or suppress specific concepts without modifying the language model.
The proposed MonoSemanticity score aligns well with human perception of similarity, as validated by a large-scale user study.
papers.limitation:
