This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
papers.research_question: Does incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improve the reconstruction-interpretability frontier? Specifically, does it improve reconstruction, maintain or improve interpretability, and learn hierarchical semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (H-SAE) architecture that explicitly models semantic hierarchy, improving reconstruction performance and interpretability while being computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improves the reconstruction-interpretability frontier, leading to better reconstruction, maintained or improved interpretability, and learned hierarchical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
H-SAEs have better reconstruction performance than standard SAEs as measured by explained variance and downstream CE loss.
H-SAEs maintain or improve interpretability, showing less feature absorption and fewer redundant features across languages.
The H-SAE architecture learns hierarchical semantics, with high-level features capturing general concepts and low-level features capturing specific instances.
The hierarchical structure provides significant computational efficiency gains, allowing scaling to larger effective dictionary sizes with minimal overhead.
The architecture successfully translates theoretical insights about hierarchical concept geometry into a practical mixture-of-experts type model.
papers.limitation: Results are still imperfect, with some hard-to-interpret features and far from perfect reconstruction.
future_direction: Explore other reconstruction objectives beyond Euclidean distance.
Incorporate insights from causal representation learning into LLM interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.

papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: Training Superior Sparse Autoencoders for Instruct Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on instruct models, given that existing methods designed for base models result in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Finetuning-aligned Sequential Training (FAST), a novel method for training sparse autoencoders on instruct models that aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns of instruct models, leading to significant improvements in reconstruction quality and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: FAST is an effective method for training SAEs on instruct models, achieving superior reconstruction and feature interpretability, and the resulting SAEs can be used to steer model behavior via special token features, opening new avenues for model control.
papers.key_findings:
FAST significantly outperforms baseline Block Training methods (BT(P) and BT(F)) in token reconstruction (MSE) and special token reconstruction (MSEst) across multiple instruct models and SAE architectures.
FAST produces a higher proportion of high-quality, interpretable features compared to baseline methods, as measured by an automated feature interpretability scoring framework.
Intervening on the activations of special tokens via the trained SAEs can improve output quality and enable fine-grained control of model behavior, suggesting new applications for SAEs.
future_direction: Exploring the opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior through steering with SAE latents, particularly via special tokens.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow in scale and capability, understanding their internal mechanisms becomes increasingly critical. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a key tool in mechanistic interpretability, enabling the extraction of human-interpretable features from LLMs. However, existing SAE training methods are primarily designed for base models, resulting in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability when applied to instruct models. To bridge this gap, we propose $\underline{\textbf{F}}$inetuning-$\underline{\textbf{a}}$ligned $\underline{\textbf{S}}$equential $\underline{\textbf{T}}$raining ($\textit{FAST}$), a novel training method specifically tailored for instruct models. $\textit{FAST}$ aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns characteristic of instruct models, resulting in substantial improvements in both reconstruction and feature interpretability. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, $\textit{FAST}$ achieves a mean squared error of 0.6468 in token reconstruction, significantly outperforming baseline methods with errors of 5.1985 and 1.5096. In feature interpretability, $\textit{FAST}$ yields a higher proportion of high-quality features, for Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, $21.1\%$ scored in the top range, compared to $7.0\%$ and $10.2\%$ for $\textit{BT(P)}$ and $\textit{BT(F)}$. Surprisingly, we discover that intervening on the activations of special tokens via the SAEs leads to improvements in output quality, suggesting new opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior. Code, data, and 240 trained SAEs are available at https://github.com/Geaming2002/FAST.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Insights on Voice Embeddings
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract mono-semantic features from non-textual embedded data, specifically speaker embeddings from a Titanet model?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can effectively extract mono-semantic features from non-textual speaker embeddings, demonstrating characteristics like feature splitting and steering similar to LLM embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are effective for extracting mono-semantic features from non-textual embedded data, suggesting their utility for interpreting embeddings in domains like audio-based speaker recognition.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders identify mono-semantic features such as language and music from Titanet speaker embeddings with high precision and recall.
Features exhibit splitting behavior as latent space grows, e.g., Spanish language feature splits into male and female sub-features.
Feature steering by manipulating latent activations can shift embeddings towards or away from reference classes, as shown with Spanish/English and music/voice.
The autoencoder reflects the training data distribution, with features like Spanish appearing as deviations from the default English.
Model parameters like latent dimension and TopK value affect feature identification performance, with higher recall at lower dimensions and higher K-values.
papers.limitation:
Shortage of clearly discrete features in audio data compared to text, making labeling continuous features like gender difficult.
Latent to embedding dimension ratio is much smaller than in LLM studies due to data limitations, potentially limiting feature extraction.
future_direction: Exploring the universality of mono-semantic features across different speaker embedding models.
Investigating the application of sparse autoencoders to Whisper embeddings to capture both linguistic and audio characteristics.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in explainable machine learning have highlighted the potential of sparse autoencoders in uncovering mono-semantic features in densely encoded embeddings. While most research has focused on Large Language Model (LLM) embeddings, the applicability of this technique to other domains remains largely unexplored. This study applies sparse autoencoders to speaker embeddings generated from a Titanet model, demonstrating the effectiveness of this technique in extracting mono-semantic features from non-textual embedded data. The results show that the extracted features exhibit characteristics similar to those found in LLM embeddings, including feature splitting and steering. The analysis reveals that the autoencoder can identify and manipulate features such as language and music, which are not evident in the original embedding. The findings suggest that sparse autoencoders can be a valuable tool for understanding and interpreting embedded data in many domains, including audio-based speaker recognition.

papers.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Why do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) underperform relative to other techniques, and can we fix the problems? Specifically, the paper investigates the problem of 'feature hedging' in narrow SAEs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'feature hedging' as a fundamental problem in narrow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) where correlated features are merged, degrading monosemanticity, and proposes an improved variant called balance matryoshka SAEs to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Feature hedging is a core theoretical problem in SAEs that contributes to their underperformance, and the proposed balance matryoshka SAE architecture is a step towards addressing both hedging and absorption, though both problems remain.
papers.key_findings:
Feature hedging occurs when an SAE is too narrow to represent all underlying features and features are correlated, causing the SAE to merge components of correlated features into single latents.
Hedging is caused by the reconstruction (MSE) loss and becomes more severe the narrower the SAE.
In LLM SAEs, hedging is likely the norm due to the high number of correlated features and the SAE being narrower than the number of underlying features.
Balance matryoshka SAEs, which tune the relative loss coefficients between inner and outer levels, can improve performance by better balancing the competing forces of hedging and absorption.
SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging, while wider SAEs suffer more from absorption.
papers.limitation: Only test hedging in SAEs up to 65k latents on LLMs with 2b parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Improving balance matryoshka SAEs by learning different balancing coefficients per latent rather than a single coefficient for all latents.
papers.abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.

papers.title: Evaluating and Designing Sparse Autoencoders by Approximating Quasi-Orthogonality
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be evaluated and designed with a theoretical grounding for sparsity, avoiding the need to manually tune the hyperparameter k?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Approximate Feature Activation (AFA), a theoretical framework linking input embedding norms to sparse feature activation norms, and top-AFA, an activation function that adaptively selects the number of active features per input without tuning k.
papers.conclusion: The AFA framework addresses a core limitation in SAE design by providing a principled way to link input embeddings to feature activations, and top-AFA SAE demonstrates improved performance over fixed-sparsity methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed top-AFA SAE outperforms top-k and batch top-k SAEs in reconstruction performance on GPT-2 layers.
The εLBO metric provides a different evaluation perspective on SAE quality compared to mean squared error (MSE).
The AFA formulation provides a closed-form estimate of the ℓ2-norm of sparse activations with provable error bounds.
Pre-trained SAE decoders often fail to achieve the level of quasi-orthogonality permitted by the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.
Top-AFA allows adaptive per-input sparsity, removing the need for a fixed sparsity hyperparameter k.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis is limited to the linear representation hypothesis; extending AFA to more general superposition settings remains an open question.
Top-AFA introduces a new hyperparameter λAFA and can result in high ℓ0 values.
future_direction: Extending AFA to more general superposition settings, such as when Φ(·) is a two-layer neural network or other SAE variants like Matryoshka SAEs.
A deeper investigation into the necessity of the loss coefficient λAFA.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used in mechanistic interpretability research for large language models; however, the state-of-the-art method of using $k$-sparse autoencoders lacks a theoretical grounding for selecting the hyperparameter $k$ that represents the number of nonzero activations, often denoted by $\ell_0$. In this paper, we reveal a theoretical link that the $\ell_2$-norm of the sparse feature vector can be approximated with the $\ell_2$-norm of the dense vector with a closed-form error, which allows sparse autoencoders to be trained without the need to manually determine $\ell_0$. Specifically, we validate two applications of our theoretical findings. First, we introduce a new methodology that can assess the feature activations of pre-trained SAEs by computing the theoretically expected value from the input embedding, which has been overlooked by existing SAE evaluation methods and loss functions. Second, we introduce a novel activation function, top-AFA, which builds upon our formulation of approximate feature activation (AFA). This function enables top-$k$ style activation without requiring a constant hyperparameter $k$ to be tuned, dynamically determining the number of activated features for each input. By training SAEs on three intermediate layers to reconstruct GPT2 hidden embeddings for over 80 million tokens from the OpenWebText dataset, we demonstrate the empirical merits of this approach and compare it with current state-of-the-art $k$-sparse autoencoders. Our code is available at: https://github.com/SewoongLee/top-afa-sae.

papers.title: Enhancing Neural Network Interpretability with Feature-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the feature learning of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to better align with input features, thereby enhancing their usefulness for neural network interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Mutual Feature Regularization (MFR), a regularization technique that trains multiple Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) in parallel with weight reinitialization and an auxiliary penalty to encourage learning similar features, leading to better alignment with input features and improved SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: MFR encourages SAEs to learn more features of the input, thereby increasing their usefulness for neural network interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MFR increases the correlation between feature similarity across SAEs and similarity with input features, as demonstrated on synthetic data.
On synthetic data, SAEs trained with MFR recover more of the known input features compared to baseline SAEs.
MFR improves reconstruction loss and loss recovered when training SAEs on GPT-2 Small MLP layer activations, with up to a 21.21% reduction in reconstruction loss.
MFR also improves reconstruction loss on EEG denoising tasks, though the benefits are smaller than for neural network activations.
The method involves conditionally reinitializing SAE weights based on inactive feature detection and adding an auxiliary penalty to encourage feature similarity across SAEs.
papers.limitation: MFR increases computational cost as it requires training multiple SAEs in parallel, which may become unmanageable for very large models.
future_direction: Investigate efficient mutual learning-based approaches for SAEs that can benefit from the positive relationship between feature similarity across SAEs and feature similarity with input features without requiring more compute.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in improving the interpretability of neural network activations, but can learn features that are not features of the input, limiting their effectiveness. We propose \textsc{Mutual Feature Regularization} \textbf{(MFR)}, a regularization technique for improving feature learning by encouraging SAEs trained in parallel to learn similar features. We motivate \textsc{MFR} by showing that features learned by multiple SAEs are more likely to correlate with features of the input. By training on synthetic data with known features of the input, we show that \textsc{MFR} can help SAEs learn those features, as we can directly compare the features learned by the SAE with the input features for the synthetic data. We then scale \textsc{MFR} to SAEs that are trained to denoise electroencephalography (EEG) data and SAEs that are trained to reconstruct GPT-2 Small activations. We show that \textsc{MFR} can improve the reconstruction loss of SAEs by up to 21.21\% on GPT-2 Small, and 6.67\% on EEG data. Our results suggest that the similarity between features learned by different SAEs can be leveraged to improve SAE training, thereby enhancing performance and the usefulness of SAEs for model interpretability.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: Do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) improve performance on LLM activation probing tasks in challenging regimes such as data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift?
papers.core_contribution: SAE probes do not consistently outperform baseline probing methods across various challenging regimes, and baseline methods can achieve similar interpretability insights.
papers.conclusion: Current SAEs do not offer a consistent advantage for probing tasks, highlighting the need for rigorous evaluation of interpretability methods with strong baselines.
papers.key_findings:
SAE probes underperform baseline logistic regression on average across datasets in standard conditions.
SAE probes do not provide a consistent advantage in data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift regimes.
Baseline methods can provide similar interpretability insights as SAE probes, such as detecting dataset issues.
Pruning SAE latents based on autointerp descriptions can slightly improve out-of-distribution generalization but not enough to match the performance drop.
SAE latents sometimes fail to generalize out-of-distribution, e.g., a latent for 'living room' only fires on English phrases.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to probing tasks and may not generalize to other tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for interpreting concepts represented in large language model (LLM) activations. However, there is a lack of evidence regarding the validity of their interpretations due to the lack of a ground truth for the concepts used by an LLM, and a growing number of works have presented problems with current SAEs. One alternative source of evidence would be demonstrating that SAEs improve performance on downstream tasks beyond existing baselines. We test this by applying SAEs to the real-world task of LLM activation probing in four regimes: data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift. Due to the difficulty of detecting concepts in these challenging settings, we hypothesize that SAEs' basis of interpretable, concept-level latents should provide a useful inductive bias. However, although SAEs occasionally perform better than baselines on individual datasets, we are unable to design ensemble methods combining SAEs with baselines that consistently outperform ensemble methods solely using baselines. Additionally, although SAEs initially appear promising for identifying spurious correlations, detecting poor dataset quality, and training multi-token probes, we are able to achieve similar results with simple non-SAE baselines as well. Though we cannot discount SAEs' utility on other tasks, our findings highlight the shortcomings of current SAEs and the need to rigorously evaluate interpretability methods on downstream tasks with strong baselines.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Antibody Language Models Using SAEs
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal interpretable features in antibody language models and be used to steer generation? How do TopK and Ordered SAEs compare in terms of interpretability and steerability?
papers.core_contribution: TopK SAEs can identify interpretable features in antibody language models but are not steerable, while Ordered SAEs can identify steerable features but with less interpretable activation patterns, suggesting Ordered SAEs are preferable for generative steering.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are effective for interpretability and steering in antibody language models, with trade-offs between interpretability and steerability between TopK and Ordered SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs can reveal biologically meaningful latent features in antibody language models.
High feature-concept correlation in TopK SAEs does not guarantee causal control over generation.
Ordered SAEs impose a hierarchical structure that reliably identifies steerable features.
Ordered SAEs come at the expense of more complex and less interpretable activation patterns.
SAEs can be used to incorporate rational design principles into antibody library generation.
papers.limitation:
Lack of labelled datasets for antibodies compared to general proteins, which prevents automated feature identification and annotation.
TopK SAEs may not consistently generate monosemantic features for all concepts.
future_direction: Conduct exhaustive steering analyses to quantitatively measure the steerability of Top-K and Ordered SAE features.
Scale SAE training using more expansive, annotated datasets like FLAb to enable models to identify domain-specific abstractions.
Use SAEs to generate antibody libraries with properties such as developability and specificity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a mechanistic interpretability technique that have been used to provide insight into learned concepts within large protein language models. Here, we employ TopK and Ordered SAEs to investigate an autoregressive antibody language model, p-IgGen, and steer its generation. We show that TopK SAEs can reveal biologically meaningful latent features, but high feature concept correlation does not guarantee causal control over generation. In contrast, Ordered SAEs impose an hierarchical structure that reliably identifies steerable features, but at the expense of more complex and less interpretable activation patterns. These findings advance the mechanistic interpretability of domain-specific protein language models and suggest that, while TopK SAEs are sufficient for mapping latent features to concepts, Ordered SAEs are preferable when precise generative steering is required.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can find a canonical set of units of analysis (unique, complete, and atomic features) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis because smaller SAEs are incomplete (missing information) and larger SAEs learn composed, non-atomic features. The choice of SAE dictionary size should be pragmatic.
papers.conclusion: Alternative methods are required for identifying canonical units of analysis, and SAE practitioners should adopt a pragmatic approach to choosing dictionary size for interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE stitching reveals that larger SAEs contain novel latents that improve reconstruction when added to smaller SAEs, indicating smaller SAEs are incomplete.
SAE stitching shows that larger SAEs also contain reconstruction latents similar to those in smaller SAEs, but sometimes composed of multiple smaller latents.
Meta-SAEs can decompose larger SAE latents into interpretable meta-latents, demonstrating that larger SAE latents are not atomic.
Meta-latents are similar to latents found in smaller SAEs, suggesting larger SAE latents are compositions of smaller SAE latents.
The sparsity penalty in SAEs incentivizes the learning of composed features in larger dictionaries, rather than atomic features.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines two language models (GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B) and does not include very large SAEs.
Associating SAE latents with interpretable concepts remains an open problem, and the methods do not identify canonical units nor the optimal dictionary size.
future_direction: Pursue different approaches for identifying canonical units of analysis.
Pragmatically choose SAE dictionary size based on the specific interpretability task.
papers.abstract: A common goal of mechanistic interpretability is to decompose the activations of neural networks into features: interpretable properties of the input computed by the model. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for finding these features in LLMs, and it has been postulated that they can be used to find a \textit{canonical} set of units: a unique and complete list of atomic features. We cast doubt on this belief using two novel techniques: SAE stitching to show they are incomplete, and meta-SAEs to show they are not atomic. SAE stitching involves inserting or swapping latents from a larger SAE into a smaller one. Latents from the larger SAE can be divided into two categories: \emph{novel latents}, which improve performance when added to the smaller SAE, indicating they capture novel information, and \emph{reconstruction latents}, which can replace corresponding latents in the smaller SAE that have similar behavior. The existence of novel features indicates incompleteness of smaller SAEs. Using meta-SAEs -- SAEs trained on the decoder matrix of another SAE -- we find that latents in SAEs often decompose into combinations of latents from a smaller SAE, showing that larger SAE latents are not atomic. The resulting decompositions are often interpretable; e.g. a latent representing ``Einstein'' decomposes into ``scientist'', ``Germany'', and ``famous person''. Even if SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis, they may still be useful tools. We suggest that future research should either pursue different approaches for identifying such units, or pragmatically choose the SAE size suited to their task. We provide an interactive dashboard to explore meta-SAEs: https://metasaes.streamlit.app/

papers.title: OrtSAE: Orthogonal Sparse Autoencoders Uncover Atomic Features
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate feature absorption and composition in sparse autoencoders to learn more atomic, interpretable features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OrtSAE, a sparse autoencoder training method that enforces orthogonality between decoder features to reduce feature absorption and composition, yielding more atomic and interpretable features with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: OrtSAE effectively addresses feature absorption and composition in sparse autoencoders through orthogonal constraints, producing more atomic features while preserving reconstruction fidelity and downstream task performance with minimal computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
OrtSAE discovers 9% more distinct features than traditional SAEs.
OrtSAE reduces feature absorption by 65% and feature composition by 15% compared to traditional SAEs.
OrtSAE improves performance on spurious correlation removal by 6% while maintaining on-par performance on other downstream tasks.
OrtSAE achieves feature orthogonality near random initialization levels, significantly lower than other SAE variants.
OrtSAE decomposes composite features from traditional SAEs into more atomic components, as shown qualitatively.
future_direction: Investigate using orthogonal features as more interpretable building blocks for neural circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a technique for sparse decomposition of neural network activations into human-interpretable features. However, current SAEs suffer from feature absorption, where specialized features capture instances of general features creating representation holes, and feature composition, where independent features merge into composite representations. In this work, we introduce Orthogonal SAE (OrtSAE), a novel approach aimed to mitigate these issues by enforcing orthogonality between the learned features. By implementing a new training procedure that penalizes high pairwise cosine similarity between SAE features, OrtSAE promotes the development of disentangled features while scaling linearly with the SAE size, avoiding significant computational overhead. We train OrtSAE across different models and layers and compare it with other methods. We find that OrtSAE discovers 9% more distinct features, reduces feature absorption (by 65%) and composition (by 15%), improves performance on spurious correlation removal (+6%), and achieves on-par performance for other downstream tasks compared to traditional SAEs.

papers.title: Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
papers.research_question: How can we control fine-grained reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models using Sparse Autoencoders to overcome concept entanglement and improve reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-Steering, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders to disentangle and identify strategy-specific features for controlling reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models, achieving superior control effectiveness and error correction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can disentangle strategy-specific features for fine-grained control of reasoning strategies, with SAE-Steering providing an efficient feature identification pipeline that is effective and robust.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Steering outperforms existing control methods by over 15% in control effectiveness across various reasoning tasks and models.
The identified SAE features generalize from math to science domains, indicating cross-domain applicability.
Logit-based feature recall is more precise than activation-based methods, improving feature selection accuracy.
Strategy-specific features are prevalent in deeper layers of the model, with optimal control effectiveness in middle-to-late layers.
Controlling reasoning strategies can redirect models from erroneous paths, achieving a 7% absolute accuracy improvement in error correction.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated five representative reasoning strategies
Only demonstrated application in error correction scenarios
Only attempted to correct erroneous paths by enforcing continued reasoning
future_direction: Investigate controlling other reasoning strategies
Explore applying control to a wider range of applications
Explore guiding the LRM at earlier stages or during intermediate steps
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit human-like cognitive reasoning strategies (e.g. backtracking, cross-verification) during reasoning process, which improves their performance on complex tasks. Currently, reasoning strategies are autonomously selected by LRMs themselves. However, such autonomous selection often produces inefficient or even erroneous reasoning paths. To make reasoning more reliable and flexible, it is important to develop methods for controlling reasoning strategies. Existing methods struggle to control fine-grained reasoning strategies due to conceptual entanglement in LRMs' hidden states. To address this, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose strategy-entangled hidden states into a disentangled feature space. To identify the few strategy-specific features from the vast pool of SAE features, we propose SAE-Steering, an efficient two-stage feature identification pipeline. SAE-Steering first recalls features that amplify the logits of strategy-specific keywords, filtering out over 99\% of features, and then ranks the remaining features by their control effectiveness. Using the identified strategy-specific features as control vectors, SAE-Steering outperforms existing methods by over 15\% in control effectiveness. Furthermore, controlling reasoning strategies can redirect LRMs from erroneous paths to correct ones, achieving a 7\% absolute accuracy improvement.

papers.title: Interpretable Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders: A Data Analysis Toolkit
papers.research_question: How can we analyze large-scale text corpora in a cost-effective and controllable way? The paper proposes using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to create interpretable embeddings for data analysis.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE embeddings, a method using sparse autoencoders to create interpretable embeddings from text, which are more cost-effective and controllable than LLM-based labeling and dense embeddings for data analysis tasks like dataset diffing, correlation discovery, clustering, and retrieval.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a versatile tool for textual data analysis, providing a cost-effective and controllable alternative to LLM-based methods and dense embeddings. The work demonstrates the value of using data to interpret models.
papers.key_findings:
SAE embeddings identify larger frequency differences between datasets at 2-8x lower cost than LLM-based methods.
SAE embeddings reliably discover unexpected correlations between concepts in text, revealing biases and artifacts.
Filtering SAE embeddings to specific concepts enables targeted clustering along axes of interest, uncovering novel groupings not found by dense embeddings.
SAE embeddings match or outperform dense embeddings on property-based retrieval tasks.
Case studies using SAE embeddings reveal model behaviors, such as Grok-4's tendency to clarify ambiguities and Tulu-3's learned trigger phrases.
papers.limitation: SAE latent descriptions can generalize poorly to unseen texts, affecting their reliability as data labelers on out-of-distribution data.
papers.abstract: Analyzing large-scale text corpora is a core challenge in machine learning, crucial for tasks like identifying undesirable model behaviors or biases in training data. Current methods often rely on costly LLM-based techniques (e.g. annotating dataset differences) or dense embedding models (e.g. for clustering), which lack control over the properties of interest. We propose using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to create SAE embeddings: representations whose dimensions map to interpretable concepts. Through four data analysis tasks, we show that SAE embeddings are more cost-effective and reliable than LLMs and more controllable than dense embeddings. Using the large hypothesis space of SAEs, we can uncover insights such as (1) semantic differences between datasets and (2) unexpected concept correlations in documents. For instance, by comparing model responses, we find that Grok-4 clarifies ambiguities more often than nine other frontier models. Relative to LLMs, SAE embeddings uncover bigger differences at 2-8x lower cost and identify biases more reliably. Additionally, SAE embeddings are controllable: by filtering concepts, we can (3) cluster documents along axes of interest and (4) outperform dense embeddings on property-based retrieval. Using SAE embeddings, we study model behavior with two case studies: investigating how OpenAI model behavior has changed over time and finding "trigger" phrases learned by Tulu-3 (Lambert et al., 2024) from its training data. These results position SAEs as a versatile tool for unstructured data analysis and highlight the neglected importance of interpreting models through their data.

papers.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we align Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features with human-defined concepts to create an interpretable and controllable interface for Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: ALIGNSAE is a method that aligns Sparse Autoencoder features with a predefined ontology through a two-stage training curriculum, enabling precise concept-level inspection and control in frozen LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ALIGNSAE provides a verifiable and controllable interface for concept-level manipulation in LLMs, advancing interpretability and steering capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ALIGNSAE achieves near-perfect concept-slot binding in mid-layers (e.g., layer 6) of GPT-2, with diagonal accuracy up to 1.00.
It significantly reduces concept fragmentation and increases top-1 concentration compared to traditional unsupervised SAEs.
Swap interventions demonstrate reliable controllability with a clear fidelity-strength tradeoff, achieving up to 0.847 swap success at layer 6.
In 2-hop reasoning, ALIGNSAE attains 4× higher swap success than traditional SAE.
The method provides mechanistic insights into grokking-like generalization dynamics via step-wise concept binding.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on a limited ontology (6 relations for 1-hop, 20 for 2-hop) and on GPT-2, a relatively small model, which may not reflect performance on larger models or more complex ontologies.
Swap controllability has a narrow effective amplification range (around α=2), and over-amplification can destabilize interventions.
future_direction: Extending ALIGNSAE to larger ontologies and more complex concept types.
Applying the method to larger language models and more diverse tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

papers.title: Don't Forget It! Conditional Sparse Autoencoder Clamping Works for Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders be used to unlearn harmful knowledge in large language models while retaining safe knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a conditional SAE-based clamping method for unlearning that improves retention of safe information compared to prior SAE methods and performs comparably to RMU with better interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning outperforms prior SAE approaches on retention and performs comparably with RMU on forgetting harmful information while retaining safe information, with fewer hyperparameters and better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal Clamp achieves the lowest WMDP-bio accuracy (0.2718) and highest alignment score (0.8226), indicating effective unlearning with some impact on general knowledge.
Clamp Prime improves forgetting performance (WMDP-bio accuracy drops to 0.2985) but slightly reduces general knowledge retention compared to RMU.
Adversarial evaluation using Concurrent Greedy Search shows that unlearned models resist suffix attacks, continuing to output gibberish.
The method requires fewer hyperparameter choices than RMU while maintaining interpretability.
SAE-based unlearning is shown to be viable, with conditional steering reducing side effects on safe information.
papers.limitation:
Training sparse autoencoders and labeling the latents is slow and expensive, limiting practicality to models with pre-existing SAEs.
Steering models with sparse autoencoders requires closed weights, as attackers can remove steering hooks if they have access to the weights.
Using Wikitext as the retain set for RMU may cause bias, potentially inflating the method's score on biology-related subjects in evaluation.
future_direction: Investigating which SAE layers allow for the best unlearning.
Exploring the impact of latent space dimensionality (i.e., using SAEs with larger hidden activation shapes).
Training interpretable parameters that edit the SAE latent vector to allow for fully interpretable fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in Large Language Model (LLM) capabilities have brought great potential but also posed new risks. For example, LLMs with knowledge of bioweapons, advanced chemistry, or cyberattacks could cause violence if placed in the wrong hands or during malfunctions. Because of their nature as near-black boxes, intuitive interpretation of LLM internals remains an open research question, preventing developers from easily controlling model behavior and capabilities. The use of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) has recently emerged as a potential method of unraveling representations of concepts in LLMs internals, and has allowed developers to steer model outputs by directly modifying the hidden activations. In this paper, we use SAEs to identify unwanted concepts from the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset within gemma-2-2b internals and use feature steering to reduce the model's ability to answer harmful questions while retaining its performance on harmless queries. Our results bring back optimism to the viability of SAE-based explicit knowledge unlearning techniques.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
DSG is highly data-efficient and can perform zero-shot unlearning by leveraging semantically relevant SAE features identified without task-specific data.
DSG provides interpretable unlearning by targeting specific, semantically coherent SAE features associated with the knowledge to be removed.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is a promising approach to improve LLM safety by removing unwanted knowledge from the model. However, prevailing gradient-based unlearning methods suffer from issues such as high computational costs, hyperparameter instability, poor sequential unlearning capability, vulnerability to relearning attacks, low data efficiency, and lack of interpretability. While Sparse Autoencoders are well-suited to improve these aspects by enabling targeted activation-based unlearning, prior approaches underperform gradient-based methods. This work demonstrates that, contrary to these earlier findings, SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when employed dynamically. We introduce $\textbf{Dynamic DAE Guardrails}$ (DSG), a novel method for precision unlearning that leverages principled feature selection and a dynamic classifier. Our experiments show DSG substantially outperforms leading unlearning methods, achieving superior forget-utility trade-offs. DSG addresses key drawbacks of gradient-based approaches for unlearning -- offering enhanced computational efficiency and stability, robust performance in sequential unlearning, stronger resistance to relearning attacks, better data efficiency including zero-shot settings, and more interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: On the transferability of Sparse Autoencoders for interpreting compressed models
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) trained on uncompressed models be effectively transferred to interpret compressed (pruned) models, and is pruning the original SAE itself a viable alternative to training a new SAE on the pruned model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs pretrained on uncompressed models can be transferred to pruned models with minimal performance loss, and pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, offering a computationally efficient alternative.
papers.conclusion: Retraining SAEs for each compressed model variant may be unnecessary; pruning the pretrained SAE offers a practical and computationally efficient alternative for post-hoc interpretability analysis of compressed models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model with only slight performance degradation compared to SAEs trained on the compressed model.
Pruning a pretrained SAE (e.g., to 25% sparsity) yields performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, eliminating the need for costly retraining.
The transferability and pruning effectiveness hold across different model architectures (GPT-2 and Gemma-2-2B) and across various interpretability metrics (reconstruction, feature absorption, SCR, TPP, RAVEL).
future_direction: Explore the generalization of these findings to quantized and low-rank compressed models.
Further investigate the role of pruning as an implicit regularizer in interpretability systems.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs face inference efficiency challenges due to their scale. To address this, many compression methods have been proposed, such as pruning and quantization. However, the effect of compression on a model's interpretability remains elusive. While several model interpretation approaches exist, such as circuit discovery, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have proven particularly effective in decomposing a model's activation space into its feature basis. In this work, we explore the differences in SAEs for the original and compressed models. We find that SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model albeit with slight performance degradation compared to the trained SAE on the compressed model. Furthermore, simply pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model. This finding enables us to mitigate the extensive training costs of SAEs.

papers.title: Route Sparse Autoencoder to Interpret Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively extract interpretable features from multiple layers of a large language model, overcoming the limitations of single-layer sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Route Sparse Autoencoder (RouteSAE), a framework that integrates a lightweight routing mechanism with a shared sparse autoencoder to dynamically and efficiently extract interpretable features from multiple layers of a language model's residual stream.
papers.conclusion: RouteSAE is a powerful tool for understanding and intervening in the internal representations of LLMs, providing a scalable and effective method for feature discovery and interpretability-driven model interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Under the same sparsity constraint, RouteSAE extracts 22.5% more interpretable features than baseline SAEs while achieving a 22.3% higher interpretability score.
RouteSAE achieves a lower KL divergence at the same sparsity level compared to baseline SAEs, indicating better reconstruction quality and feature relevance for language modeling.
RouteSAE successfully captures both low-level features (e.g., word-level polysemy) from shallow layers and high-level features (e.g., sentence-level patterns) from deep layers within a unified feature space.
The routing mechanism assigns weights in a U-shaped distribution across layers, balancing the use of shallow and deep layers rather than concentrating on a subset.
RouteSAE enables targeted feature steering by manipulating feature activations, allowing controlled intervention on the model's output behavior.
papers.limitation:
The router employs a simple linear projection, which has limited capabilities; its weight distribution is influenced by the feature space size and sparsity level.
The current method of dynamically selecting activations across layers is not yet optimized for discovering cross-layer features.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated activation aggregation methods and router designs.
Enabling RouteSAE to more effectively identify and utilize cross-layer features.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models (LLMs) aims to uncover the internal processes of information propagation and reasoning. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have demonstrated promise in this domain by extracting interpretable and monosemantic features. However, prior works primarily focus on feature extraction from a single layer, failing to effectively capture activations that span multiple layers. In this paper, we introduce Route Sparse Autoencoder (RouteSAE), a new framework that integrates a routing mechanism with a shared SAE to efficiently extract features from multiple layers. It dynamically assigns weights to activations from different layers, incurring minimal parameter overhead while achieving high interpretability and flexibility for targeted feature manipulation. We evaluate RouteSAE through extensive experiments on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Specifically, under the same sparsity constraint of 64, RouteSAE extracts 22.5% more features than baseline SAEs while achieving a 22.3% higher interpretability score. These results underscore the potential of RouteSAE as a scalable and effective method for LLM interpretability, with applications in feature discovery and model intervention. Our codes are available at https://github.com/swei2001/RouteSAEs.

papers.title: Analysis of Variational Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE) and finds that it underperforms standard SAEs due to excessive KL divergence regularization causing feature death, disproving the hypothesis that variational methods improve feature organization.
papers.conclusion: The naive application of variational methods to sparse autoencoders does not improve feature organization or interpretability and is not a promising direction for SAE development.
papers.key_findings:
The vSAE underperforms the standard TopK SAE across core metrics like CE loss, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
The vSAE exhibits catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to KL divergence pressure pushing activations toward zero.
The vSAE shows improved performance on Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR) and Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) benchmarks, indicating more independent features.
t-SNE visualizations reveal that vSAE features are more dispersed and less clustered than SAE features, supporting the dispersive pressure hypothesis.
Despite having far fewer active features, the vSAE maintains feature interpretability, but the overall performance degradation suggests variational methods are not beneficial for SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The vSAE suffers from catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to excessive KL divergence regularization.
The observed improvements in feature independence (SCR, TPP) may be an artifact of the reduced dictionary size rather than principled organization.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach for interpreting neural network representations by learning sparse, human-interpretable features from dense activations. We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability. We introduce the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE), which replaces deterministic ReLU gating with stochastic sampling from learned Gaussian posteriors and incorporates KL divergence regularization toward a standard normal prior. Our hypothesis is that this probabilistic sampling creates dispersive pressure, causing features to organize more coherently in the latent space while avoiding overlap. We evaluate a TopK vSAE against a standard TopK SAE on Pythia-70M transformer residual stream activations using comprehensive benchmarks including SAE Bench, individual feature interpretability analysis, and global latent space visualization through t-SNE. The vSAE underperforms standard SAE across core evaluation metrics, though excels at feature independence and ablation metrics. The KL divergence term creates excessive regularization pressure that substantially reduces the fraction of living features, leading to observed performance degradation. While vSAE features demonstrate improved robustness, they exhibit many more dead features than baseline. Our findings suggest that naive application of variational methods to SAEs does not improve feature organization or interpretability.

papers.title: CRISP: Persistent Concept Unlearning via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to achieve persistent concept unlearning in large language models using sparse autoencoders to remove harmful knowledge while maintaining model utility.
papers.core_contribution: CRISP is a parameter-efficient method for persistent concept unlearning in LLMs using sparse autoencoders, achieving state-of-the-art performance by selectively suppressing harmful features while preserving benign knowledge and fluency.
papers.conclusion: CRISP is an effective sparse autoencoder-based method for persistent unlearning in LLMs, offering improved performance and interpretability through feature-level suppression.
papers.key_findings:
CRISP outperforms prior methods like ELM and RMU on WMDP benchmarks, with higher overall scores.
It maintains better fluency and concept scores after unlearning, as shown in qualitative and quantitative evaluations.
Feature analysis reveals that CRISP identifies semantically coherent target features for suppression, enabling precise unlearning.
CRISP demonstrates a superior trade-off between unlearning efficacy and retention of benign knowledge.
The method is effective across different models, including Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B.
papers.limitation:
Relies on pretrained SAEs, and effectiveness may diminish if SAEs fail to capture disentangled or interpretable features.
Evaluation is limited to safety-critical domains, and generalization to new tasks and domains is not yet understood.
No formal theoretical guarantees of complete knowledge removal; residual information may persist, and robustness against adversarial extraction is an open direction.
future_direction: Robustness against adversarial extraction
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the need to selectively remove unwanted knowledge while preserving model utility has become paramount. Recent work has explored sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to perform precise interventions on monosemantic features. However, most SAE-based methods operate at inference time, which does not create persistent changes in the model's parameters. Such interventions can be bypassed or reversed by malicious actors with parameter access. We introduce CRISP, a parameter-efficient method for persistent concept unlearning using SAEs. CRISP automatically identifies salient SAE features across multiple layers and suppresses their activations. We experiment with two LLMs and show that our method outperforms prior approaches on safety-critical unlearning tasks from the WMDP benchmark, successfully removing harmful knowledge while preserving general and in-domain capabilities. Feature-level analysis reveals that CRISP achieves semantically coherent separation between target and benign concepts, allowing precise suppression of the target features.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Low-$N$ Protein Function Prediction and Design
papers.research_question: How effective are sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for protein function prediction and design in low-data (low-N) regimes?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a compact and biologically meaningful latent space that improves low-N fitness prediction and enables effective protein design via latent steering, outperforming ESM2 baselines.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a powerful tool for low-N protein function prediction and design, expanding the biologist's toolkit for resource-constrained applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform ESM2 baselines in 58% of fitness extrapolation tasks with as few as 24 training sequences.
SAEs design top-fitness variants in 83% of cases via latent steering, compared to designing with ESM2 alone.
The sparse latent space of SAEs encodes biologically interpretable motifs and compresses relevant information, reducing overfitting in low-N regimes.
Analysis of steered variants reveals that SAEs activate latents corresponding to known biological motifs such as active sites, allosteric sites, and epistatic sites.
SAE performance is influenced by the number of available multiple sequence alignment (MSA) sequences for training.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to a set of proteins; it could be extended to other proteins with clinically relevant functions such as antibiotic resistance and viral replication.
SAE performance is strongly influenced by the number of MSA sequences available for training; strategies are needed for robust training when MSAs are shallow.
Protein engineering experiments rely on in-silico fitness models; wet lab validation is necessary to verify function.
